---

## 2. Purpose

This policy establishes the Heat Illness Prevention Program for Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. as required by:

- **California Code of Regulations, Title 8, §3395** — Heat Illness Prevention (applicable to outdoor places of employment)
- **California Code of Regulations, Title 8, §5141.1** — Heat Illness Prevention in Indoor Places of Employment (effective January 1, 2025)

Home health field employees are exposed to heat illness risk in two distinct environments:
1. **Outdoors** — walking to/from patient residences, traveling in vehicles, working in patient yards, community settings, or unconditioned areas adjacent to residences
2. **Indoors** — working in patient residences or other structures where ambient indoor temperature may reach or exceed 82°F due to inadequate or absent air conditioning, particularly during California heat events

Heat illness is a serious, potentially fatal condition. This program establishes procedures so that all employees of the agency have access to water, shade, cool-down rest periods, training, and effective emergency response in the event of suspected heat illness.

---

## 3. Scope

This policy applies to:

* All employees of Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. who perform work duties in outdoor environments or in indoor environments where temperatures may reach or exceed 82°F
* Job classifications primarily affected: Registered Nurse (RN), Licensed Vocational Nurse (LVN), Physical Therapist (PT), Occupational Therapist (OT), Speech-Language Pathologist (SLP), Medical Social Worker (MSW), Home Health Aide (HHA)
* All field work settings: patient residences, community clinic visits, outdoor environments during field work, vehicles used during work duties
* High-heat conditions trigger additional requirements (≥95°F outdoor ambient temperature or ≥87°F indoor ambient temperature per §5141.1)

This program also addresses vehicle heat exposure, which is a distinct risk for employees who use personal or agency vehicles in California's climate.

---

## 4. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| :---- | :---- |
| Heat Illness | A serious medical condition resulting from the body's inability to regulate its core temperature, ranging from heat cramps and heat syncope (fainting) to heat exhaustion and heat stroke. Heat stroke is a medical emergency with potential to cause death or permanent disability. |
| Ambient Temperature | The temperature of the surrounding air. For outdoor work: measured by a thermometer in the shade at the work location. For indoor work: the temperature at any workstation where employees perform work. |
| Heat Index | The apparent temperature felt by the body, accounting for temperature and relative humidity. Cal/OSHA permits use of heat index in lieu of dry-bulb temperature for §3395 compliance. |
| High-Heat Condition (Outdoor) | Periods when the outdoor ambient temperature equals or exceeds 95°F (35°C) at the work location. Triggers additional procedural requirements under §3395. |
| High-Heat Condition (Indoor) | Indoor ambient temperature at or above 87°F (30.6°C) at the workstation where employees perform work, or at or above 82°F where: employees wear clothing that restricts heat removal or employees work in a high-radiant-heat environment. Triggers requirements under §5141.1. |
| Cool-Down Rest Period | Preventive cool-down rest periods provided to employees at their request, taken in a shaded area or cool area (at or below 80°F where practicable for indoor). These periods are treated as rest breaks and are compensated. |
| Acclimatization | The physiological adaptation process by which the body adjusts to work in hot conditions. New employees and employees returning from absences greater than 14 days require a progressive acclimatization period per §3395. |
| Personal Heat Illness Risk Factors | Individual factors that increase heat illness vulnerability including: age >55, obesity, certain medications (anticholinergics, diuretics, beta-blockers, stimulants), diabetes, cardiovascular disease, prior heat illness, and wearing personal protective equipment. |

---

## 5. Policy Statement

5.1 Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. shall provide and maintain a Heat Illness Prevention Program in complete compliance with 8 CCR §3395 (outdoor workers) and 8 CCR §5141.1 (indoor workers).

5.2 The agency shall provide potable drinking water to all employees working in heat conditions, meeting the quantity and access requirements in Section 6.1.

5.3 The agency shall ensure access to shade or cooling areas for employees working outdoors in temperatures ≥80°F at all times when requested by an employee. Employees shall not be required to seek approval before taking a preventive cool-down rest period. Cool-down rest periods shall be compensated time.

5.4 The agency shall initiate an acclimatization protocol for all new employees and for any employee returning from an absence of 14 or more days who will be performing work in heat conditions.

5.5 Employees are required to report heat illness symptoms — including heavy sweating, weakness, dizziness, nausea, headache, confusion, or cessation of sweating — to their supervisor immediately. Employees shall not be discouraged or penalized for taking preventive cool-down rest periods.

5.6 For indoor work environments (patient residences) at or above 82°F: the agency shall provide employees with procedures for assessing indoor temperature, taking cool-down periods, and requesting supervisor assistance if the environment creates an unacceptable heat risk. Employees shall document indoor temperature at visits assessed as potentially heat-hazardous.

5.7 The agency shall provide heat illness prevention training to all employees before working in conditions with heat illness risk, meeting the content requirements of §3395(h) (outdoor) and §5141.1(i) (indoor).

5.8 The agency shall implement high-heat procedures whenever temperatures at or above 95°F (outdoor) or 87°F (indoor) are forecast for any location where employees will be working.

5.9 This program is a subprogram of RM-OS-001 (IIPP) and applies to all employee heat-exposure contexts.

---

## 6. Procedures

### 6.1 Water, Rest, and Shade — All Conditions

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 6.1.1 | Risk Manager / Supervisor | Ensure all field employees have access to, or carry on their person, adequate potable drinking water at all times during outdoor work or field visits in conditions ≥80°F. Adequate quantity: at least 1 quart (approximately 32 oz) of water per employee per hour of outdoor work, or equivalent access to a water source. | Continuously during outdoor work in ≥80°F conditions. |
| 6.1.2 | Field Employee | While working in high-heat conditions (≥80°F outdoor or ≥82°F indoor), drink water at frequent, regular intervals — at minimum every 15–20 minutes even if not thirsty. Do not rely on thirst as an indicator of dehydration. | Throughout heat-exposure work periods. |
| 6.1.3 | Field Employee | If working outdoors, identify shade (natural or constructed) in proximity to the work location before beginning work in temperatures ≥80°F. If no shade is available at the work location, identify a cool location (vehicle with functioning air conditioning if outdoor shade is not available) as the designated cool-down area. | Before beginning work in ≥80°F outdoor conditions. |
| 6.1.4 | Field Employee | When experiencing heat illness warning signs (dizziness, weakness, nausea, headache, irritability, clamminess, muscle cramps) — immediately move to shade or cool area and take a preventive cool-down rest period. Do not require supervisor approval; notify supervisor as soon as safely possible. | Immediately upon experiencing warning signs. |
| 6.1.5 | Supervisor | Do not impede, discourage, or penalize any employee from taking a preventive cool-down rest period. If an employee notifies a supervisor of a cool-down rest period, the supervisor shall check in on the employee within 15 minutes. | Immediately upon notification. |

### 6.2 High-Heat Procedures (Outdoor ≥95°F / Indoor ≥87°F)

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 6.2.1 | Risk Manager / Operations Manager | Monitor National Weather Service forecasts and California Excessive Heat Warning alerts daily during warm months (May–October) and on triggered days in other months. When ≥95°F is forecast for any geographic area where field staff are scheduled, activate High-Heat Procedures for affected areas. When patient home residences in that area may reach ≥87°F, activate Indoor High-Heat Procedures as well. | Daily monitoring during warm months; same-day activation when forecast is received. |
| 6.2.2 | Supervisor | When High-Heat Procedures are active: contact each assigned employee by phone at least once during the work shift to inquire about symptoms and confirm the employee has adequate water and access to shade/cooling. Document contact in the High-Heat Observation Log (Appendix A). | At least once per shift during activated High-Heat Procedures. |
| 6.2.3 | Field Employee | During High-Heat conditions: (a) increase drinking frequency — minimum 8 oz. every 20 minutes; (b) pre-wet a cooling towel or use cooling vest if provided; (c) schedule patient visits to avoid peak heat hours (10 AM–4 PM) where clinically feasible; (d) conduct patient care in the coolest available room of the residence; (e) if the residence is ≥87°F indoor and the patient lacks cooling (functional AC), document the environmental conditions and notify supervisor. | Throughout high-heat duty period. |
| 6.2.4 | Clinical Manager / Scheduler | During prolonged heat events (≥3 consecutive days of high-heat conditions), adjust field schedules where feasible to: (a) front-load visits to morning hours (before 10 AM); (b) reduce consecutive visit density for employees working without AC during visits; (c) ensure employee has adequate recovery time between visits. | During prolonged heat events; scheduling adjustments made at day-prior schedule review. |

### 6.3 Indoor Heat Assessment at Patient Residences

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 6.3.1 | Field Employee | Upon arriving at each patient residence during warm weather months (May–October) or any day when outdoor temperatures exceed 80°F: assess the indoor temperature of the work environment. If the ambient temperature (estimated) appears to be at or above 82°F: (a) document the estimated indoor temperature in the visit note; (b) identify the coolest available room for clinical activities; (c) notify supervisor if conditions appear to be ≥87°F and work duration will exceed 30 minutes. | Upon arrival at each at-risk visit. |
| 6.3.2 | Agency | Maintain a small digital thermometer in each field staff's supply kit for use in indoor temperature assessment when conditions are uncertain. Agency is not required to measure temperature at every visit, but temperature measurement shall be performed when conditions appear to be potentially hazardous. | Supply thermometers to all field clinical staff kits. |
| 6.3.3 | Field Employee | If the indoor temperature is ≥87°F and the employee will work for more than 30 minutes: (a) take a preventive cool-down period in the coolest available space (outdoors in shade if outdoors is cooler, or near open window or fan) for at least 5 minutes after every 30 minutes of clinical work; (b) notify supervisor at start of visit; (c) document cool-down periods taken and indoor temperature estimate in visit notes. | Throughout visits in ≥87°F indoor conditions. |
| 6.3.4 | Director of Nursing / Risk Manager | If repeated visits to a specific patient's residence involve sustained indoor temperatures at or above 87°F and the patient cannot secure cooling, evaluate whether the visit safety can be assured. Document assessment in the risk file and consider care plan modification (schedule change, telehealth check-in alternative for some contacts) in consultation with Clinical Manager. | Upon identification of persistent unsafe indoor heat condition. |

### 6.4 Acclimatization Protocol

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 6.4.1 | Supervisor / HR | Implement the acclimatization schedule for: (a) all new employees during their first 14 calendar days of outdoor work in heat conditions; (b) any employee returning from an absence of ≥14 calendar days who will be working in heat conditions. The progressive acclimatization schedule for new employees: Day 1–3: max 50% of normal heat-exposure duty; Day 4–7: max 70%; Day 8–14: max 90%; Day 15+: full duty. | Starting from first day of heat-exposed work for new employees; from first day back for returning employees. |
| 6.4.2 | Supervisor | Monitor all newly acclimatizing employees with increased supervisory contacts during the first 14 days: check-in by phone at a minimum at the start and end of each shift. Document check-ins on Acclimatization Monitoring Log (Appendix B). | Daily during first 14 days. |
| 6.4.3 | All Employees | Alert supervisor if experiencing heat illness symptoms during acclimatization period. The risk of heat illness is highest during the first days of heat exposure. Do not dismiss early symptoms, and escalate to emergency response if a co-worker or patient reports an employee appearing confused, not sweating in high heat, or unresponsive. | Continuously during acclimatization period. |

### 6.5 Emergency Response for Heat Illness

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 6.5.1 | Recognizing Employee or Callers | Recognize heat illness emergency warning signs: (a) loss of consciousness or unresponsiveness; (b) confusion, disorientation, slurred speech; (c) hot, dry, or flushed skin (cessation of sweating in extreme heat); (d) seizure. For ANY of these signs — CALL 911 IMMEDIATELY. Do not delay calling 911 to contact supervisor first. Move employee to shade/cool area while awaiting EMS. | Immediately upon recognizing emergency heat illness signs. |
| 6.5.2 | Responding Employee | While awaiting EMS: (a) move the affected employee to shade or cooler environment; (b) remove outer clothing if possible; (c) apply cool (not ice-cold) water to skin — wrists, armpits, neck; (d) fan the employee; (e) have employee sip cool water if conscious and able to swallow — do NOT give water to unconscious/confused persons; (f) stay with the employee until EMS arrives. | While awaiting EMS. |
| 6.5.3 | Supervisor | After being notified of a heat illness emergency: (a) confirm 911 was called; (b) notify Risk Manager and Administrator immediately; (c) contact the patient household (if incident occurred in patient home) to provide information as needed; (d) document all circumstances in the Heat Illness Incident Form (Appendix C). | Immediately upon notification. |
| 6.5.4 | Risk Manager | Following any employee heat illness incident: (a) initiate an incident investigation per RM-OS-001 Section 6.5; (b) conduct a root cause analysis per QA-AE-002; (c) identify whether program failures contributed; (d) update training or procedures within 30 days of RCA completion. | Investigation within 24 hours; RCA within 14 days; program update within 30 days. |

### 6.6 Vehicle Heat Safety

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| 6.6.1 | All Employees | Before beginning a drive in warm weather: ensure vehicle air conditioning is functional. If vehicle AC is not functional during conditions ≥80°F outdoor temperature, notify supervisor immediately — the vehicle is a heat hazard and the employee shall not perform extended driving for work assignments without functional AC or a replacement vehicle. | Before commencing each day's field duties in warm weather. |
| 6.6.2 | Risk Manager | Maintain a protocol for agency response to employee vehicle AC failure during a high-heat period: options include reschedule visits, provide rental vehicle, reassign to telephone-contact duties until vehicle is repaired. No employee shall be required to work in a vehicle without functioning AC during High-Heat conditions (≥95°F outdoor). | Protocol in place prior to warm-weather season (by May 1 each year). |
| 6.6.3 | All Employees | Never leave any person (patient, child, dependent) in an unattended vehicle in warm weather. Employees who observe a person or animal in a hot vehicle in distress are authorized and expected to call 911. | Continuously. |

### 6.7 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Excessive Heat Warning issued by NWS for service area | Risk Manager immediately notifies all supervisors and scheduling manager. | High-Heat Procedures activated; all field staff notified; visit schedule reviewed for resequencing. | Same day as warning issuance. |
| Employee self-reports heat exhaustion symptoms (not emergency) | Employee calls supervisor; supervisor activates check-in. | Employee moves to cool area; supervisor evaluates whether employee can continue. If in doubt, end field duties for the day; employee may request medical evaluation at no cost. | Immediately upon report. |
| Annual program review identifies deficiency | Risk Manager documents finding. | Corrective action plan per QA-AE-003; training update within 30 days; procedure update within 30 days. | Within 30 days. |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations

### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Written program exists, current, covers both §3395 and §5141.1 | Annual review against both regulation checklists | All elements present; reviewed within 12 months |
| All employees trained before heat-exposed work | Training log audit — training date vs. first field day | 100% trained before first heat exposure |
| High-heat procedures activated when temperature conditions met | Review of High-Heat Observation Logs vs. weather records | 100% activation on ≥95°F outdoor / ≥87°F indoor days |
| Heat illness incidents investigated within 24 hours | Review of Incident Forms | 100% investigated within 24 hours |
| Acclimatization protocol applied to new employees | Review of Acclimatization Monitoring Logs | 100% documented for all new employees during first 14 days |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For

Cal/OSHA compliance officers conducting inspection for heat-related complaints or during warm-weather enforcement initiatives will specifically verify:

1. Written Heat Illness Prevention Program exists for BOTH outdoor (§3395) and indoor (§5141.1) environments.
2. Training records confirm all employees were trained before working in heat-exposed conditions, not just at annual review.
3. High-heat procedures are documented as activated on days when threshold temperatures were met.
4. Supervisory contact logs (Appendix A) are maintained during High-Heat activations.
5. Vehicle heat safety procedures are addressed.
6. Acclimatization records for new employees are maintained.

### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Program covers outdoor only — not indoor §5141.1 (new 2025) | Citation for failure to implement §5141.1 | This program explicitly addresses both §3395 and §5141.1 |
| No supervisory check-in records during High-Heat conditions | Citation; inability to demonstrate high-heat procedure compliance | Appendix A log required and tracked on all High-Heat days |
| Acclimatization not implemented for new employees | Citation; heat illness risk | HRonboarding checklist triggers Acclimatization Protocol for all new field employees |
| Employees trained annually but not before first heat exposure | Training was provided too late | Training is triggered at hire, before first field day — not just at annual training anniversary |
| Vehicle AC failure not addressed | Employee exposed to heat illness risk in vehicle | Vehicle AC protocol per 6.6; supervisor notified if AC failure occurs during duty |

## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the comprehensive workforce training, competency validation, and policy acknowledgment program for Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. This policy ensures all workforce members receive required training across all regulatory domains (HIPAA, OSHA, infection control, fraud/waste/abuse, CMS CoP, California-specific requirements), that competency is validated through defined assessment methods, that all training is tracked in the Learning Management System (LMS), and that policy acknowledgments are documented and monitored. This policy satisfies training and competency requirements under 42 CFR Part 484, HIPAA (45 CFR § 164.530(b)), Cal/OSHA (8 CCR § 3203), and OIG Compliance Program Guidance.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all employees, contractors, per diem staff, volunteers, students, and interns of Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. All workforce members must complete required training regardless of employment status.
## 4. Policy Statements
4.1 All workforce members shall complete mandatory training per the agency's Training Requirements Matrix within the timeframes defined for each topic. The Training Requirements Matrix shall be maintained by the HR Director in consultation with the Compliance Officer, Director of Nursing, Risk Manager, and IT Director.
4.2 The following mandatory training topics are required for all workforce members at the times specified:

| Training Topic | Regulatory Basis | Initial | Annual | Triggered |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| HIPAA Privacy & Security | 45 CFR § 164.530(b); CMIA | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | Material policy change; incident involvement |
| Fraud, Waste & Abuse | OIG Guidance; Deficit Reduction Act | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | Investigation finding |
| Infection Prevention & Control | 42 CFR § 484.70; 8 CCR § 5199 | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | Outbreak event |
| OSHA / IIPP / Workplace Safety | 8 CCR § 3203; RM-OS-101 | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | New hazard identification |
| Workplace Violence Prevention (SB 553) | Cal. Lab. Code § 6401.9 | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | Post-incident |
| Bloodborne Pathogens | 8 CCR § 5193 | At assignment (clinical) | ✓ | Exposure incident |
| Emergency Preparedness | 42 CFR § 484.102 | Within 30 days of hire | ✓ | Plan revision; post-drill |
| Abuse, Neglect & Exploitation Reporting | CL-PR-006; HR-ER-009; CA Mandated Reporter | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | N/A |
| Corporate Compliance & Code of Conduct | CO-CP-001; CO-CP-004; CO-CP-008 | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | Policy revision |
| Patient Rights | 42 CFR § 484.50; CL-PR-001 | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | N/A |
| Security Awareness (IT) | IT-UP-004 | Within 14 days of hire | ✓ | Security incident |
| AI Governance (if applicable) | CO-AI-101 | Prior to first AI tool use | ✓ | Policy revision |

4.3 Clinical staff shall additionally complete discipline-specific competency evaluation per HR-TD-003 and CL-SD-008.
4.4 All training completion shall be documented in the agency's LMS. The LMS shall capture: (a) employee name and ID; (b) training topic; (c) date completed; (d) method (online, classroom, skills lab); (e) assessment score (if applicable); (f) instructor/facilitator (if applicable).
4.5 Competency validation shall be conducted through defined assessment methods appropriate to the skill or knowledge being validated: (a) written/electronic assessment (minimum passing score: 80%); (b) skills demonstration/return demonstration; (c) clinical observation; (d) case study analysis. Failed assessments require retraining and reassessment within 14 calendar days.
4.6 All workforce members shall sign a Policy Acknowledgment Form per GV-PM-003 for all policies applicable to their role: (a) within 14 calendar days of hire; (b) within 14 calendar days of any policy revision; (c) annually upon each policy's review date if re-acknowledgment is required by the policy.
4.7 Workforce members who fail to complete required training within the specified timeframe shall be subject to: (a) first occurrence — written notice with 7-day extension; (b) second occurrence — mandatory meeting with supervisor and HR; (c) third occurrence — suspension from patient care (clinical staff) or non-patient-care duties pending completion; (d) continued non-compliance — disciplinary action per HR-ER-002.

## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the employee health, occupational exposure management, and fitness-for-duty program for Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. This policy ensures compliance with California TB screening requirements (Cal. Health & Safety Code § 121525; Cal. Code Regs., tit. 17, § 2593), Cal/OSHA bloodborne pathogen exposure requirements (8 CCR § 5193), Cal/OSHA aerosol transmissible disease requirements (8 CCR § 5199), hepatitis B vaccination mandates, occupational exposure incident management, fitness-for-duty evaluation, and return-to-work clearance. This policy protects both the workforce and the patients served by ensuring that employees are medically screened, vaccinated as required, and fit to perform their duties safely.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all employees, contractors, per diem staff, students, interns, and volunteers who perform direct patient care or have occupational exposure to blood, OPIM, or aerosol transmissible pathogens.
## 4. Policy Statements
4.1 TB Screening. All employees shall undergo tuberculosis risk assessment and screening per California law (Cal. Health & Safety Code § 121525; 17 CCR § 2593):
Pre-employment: TB risk assessment and, if indicated, TB test (TST or IGRA) prior to patient contact. Employees with a positive TB test shall have a chest X-ray and medical evaluation to rule out active disease.
Annual: Annual TB risk assessment. Repeat TB testing as indicated by risk assessment or upon known exposure.
Post-exposure: TB testing within 8–10 weeks of a significant exposure to a person with suspected or confirmed active TB.
4.2 Vaccination Tracking. The agency shall maintain vaccination records for all employees with occupational exposure:
Hepatitis B: Offered within 10 working days of initial assignment per 8 CCR § 5193. Three-dose series tracked; declination documented.
Influenza: Annual vaccination recommended; declination documented.
COVID-19: Per current CDPH and CMS requirements.
Other: As required by public health order or facility-specific requirements.
4.3 Exposure Response. For all occupational exposure incidents (bloodborne, airborne, or other hazardous material):
Immediate first aid and decontamination
Medical evaluation within 24 hours (BBP) or as clinically indicated (ATD/chemical)
Source patient testing (with consent) if applicable
Employee testing per post-exposure protocol
Follow-up testing at intervals defined by the agency's Exposure Control Plan and medical provider
Workers' compensation claim initiation per HR-WM-004
4.4 Fit-for-Duty. Employees must be medically fit to perform the essential functions of their position. Fit-for-duty evaluation may be required: (a) prior to initial assignment; (b) upon return from medical leave exceeding 5 consecutive calendar days; (c) when a supervisor has documented concerns about an employee's ability to perform essential functions safely; (d) per Cal/OSHA medical surveillance requirements (e.g., respirator use medical clearance per 8 CCR § 5144).
4.5 Return-to-Work Clearance. Employees returning to duty after: (a) work-related injury or illness; (b) medical leave exceeding 5 calendar days; (c) occupational exposure requiring treatment; or (d) communicable disease must provide written medical clearance from a licensed healthcare provider specifying: (i) fitness to return to full or modified duty; (ii) any work restrictions; (iii) duration of restrictions (if any). Modified duty accommodations shall be evaluated per ADA and FEHA requirements.
## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 TB Screening

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | HR Director | Conduct TB risk assessment for all new employees using the CDPH-approved risk assessment tool. If the risk assessment indicates testing is warranted, arrange TB test (TST or IGRA). | Prior to first patient contact. |
| 6.1.2 | HR Director | For employees with positive TB test results: (a) refer for chest X-ray within 5 business days; (b) if chest X-ray is normal, document baseline and conduct annual symptom screening (no repeat X-ray unless symptomatic); (c) if chest X-ray is abnormal, refer for medical evaluation and do not permit patient contact until clearance is obtained. | Within 5 business days of positive result. |
| 6.1.3 | HR Director | Conduct annual TB risk assessment for all employees. Arrange repeat testing if indicated by risk assessment or known exposure. | Annually; per risk assessment results. |
| 6.1.4 | HR Director | Track all TB screening results in the Employee Health Tracking System. Maintain records per OSHA medical records retention (duration of employment plus 30 years). | At each screening event. |

### 6.2 Vaccination Management

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | HR Director | Offer hepatitis B vaccination series to all employees with occupational exposure within 10 working days of initial assignment. Document acceptance or declination. | Within 10 working days of assignment. |
| 6.2.2 | HR Director | Track hepatitis B vaccination series completion (3 doses). Follow up on incomplete series. If employee later reconsiders declination, offer vaccination at that time. | Per vaccination schedule (0, 1, 6 months). |
| 6.2.3 | HR Director | Coordinate annual influenza vaccination campaign. Document vaccination or declination. | Annually; during influenza season. |
| 6.2.4 | HR Director | Maintain COVID-19 vaccination records per current CDPH and CMS requirements. | Per current public health guidance. |

### 6.3 Exposure Incident Management

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Exposed Employee | Immediately perform first aid (wash wound with soap and water; flush mucous membranes with water). Report to supervisor and Risk Manager. | Immediately upon exposure. |
| 6.3.2 | Risk Manager / HR Director | Arrange confidential post-exposure medical evaluation per 8 CCR § 5193: (a) document the exposure circumstances; (b) identify and test the source individual (with consent); (c) collect exposed employee's blood for baseline testing; (d) provide post-exposure prophylaxis as recommended by medical provider. | Medical evaluation within 24 hours. |
| 6.3.3 | Risk Manager | Complete exposure incident investigation per RM-OS-101. Document on the Sharps Injury Log (if applicable). Report as required per OSHA recordkeeping. | Investigation within 72 hours. |
| 6.3.4 | HR Director | Ensure follow-up testing at intervals recommended by the medical provider (typically 6 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, 12 months for BBP). Track in Employee Health Tracking System. | Per medical provider schedule. |
| 6.3.5 | HR Director | Initiate workers' compensation claim per HR-WM-004 for all occupational exposure incidents. | Within 24 hours of incident. |

### 6.4 Fit-for-Duty and Return-to-Work

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Supervisor | When concern arises about an employee's fitness for duty, document the specific observations and consult with HR Director before initiating a fit-for-duty referral. | At the time of concern. |
| 6.4.2 | HR Director | If a fit-for-duty evaluation is warranted, arrange evaluation with the agency's occupational health provider. Provide the provider with the job description and essential functions. | Within 5 business days of determination. |
| 6.4.3 | Returning Employee | Provide written medical clearance to the HR Director specifying: (a) clearance for full or modified duty; (b) specific restrictions (if any); (c) duration of restrictions; (d) follow-up requirements. | Prior to return to duty. |
| 6.4.4 | HR Director / Supervisor | If modified duty is recommended, evaluate whether reasonable accommodation can be provided per ADA/FEHA. Document the interactive process. | Within 5 business days of receiving clearance with restrictions. |
| 6.4.5 | HR Director | Clear the employee for return to duty in the Employee Health Tracking System. Notify the supervisor. | At the time of clearance. |

# CL-OA-006 — Documentation Hierarchy and Evidence Source Prioritization
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-OA-006 |
| Policy Title | Documentation Hierarchy and Evidence Source Prioritization |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | OA — OASIS & Assessment Governance |
| Classification Tier | REQUIRED |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the priority ranking of evidence sources that authorized OASIS assessors and all clinical documentation authors at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. must apply when making clinical coding decisions, completing OASIS assessments, and creating or resolving discrepancies in clinical documentation. In home health, the same patient's clinical status may be described — sometimes differently — across multiple concurrent documentation sources: the referral discharge summary from a hospital, prior home health records from another agency, therapy evaluations, nursing visit notes from earlier in the same episode, the patient's own self-report, and the clinician's direct physical examination at the current assessment encounter. When these sources conflict, the assessor does not have discretion to simply choose the source that produces the most convenient coding result. The choice of evidence source must follow a defined, defensible, and clinically sound hierarchy that places the highest weight on contemporaneous direct clinical observation and the lowest weight on unverified secondary sources.
The absence of a documented evidence hierarchy creates three specific and serious failure modes. First, it enables financial motivation to influence source selection — an assessor who has no defined rule for choosing between sources may gravitate toward whichever source produces a higher payment group, consciously or unconsciously. Second, it creates inconsistency across assessors and across time, producing OASIS data that does not accurately represent the patient population and distorting the agency's quality measures. Third, it eliminates the audit trail that would allow the Director of Nursing, the OASIS Quality Reviewer, or a CMS surveyor to evaluate whether the assessor's coding decision was clinically sound.
This policy implements 42 CFR § 484.55(b) — which requires the comprehensive assessment to accurately reflect the patient's current health status — and the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual's foundational principle that OASIS responses must be grounded in clinical evidence collected during the assessment encounter, not inferred from external records.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All registered nurses (RNs) authorized to conduct comprehensive OASIS assessments per CL-OA-003
The OASIS Quality Reviewer who validates evidence source use during quality reviews
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager who oversees assessment accuracy
All clinical disciplines who contribute clinical information to the assessing RN during the assessment process
The Compliance Officer who reviews evidence source selection in the context of audits or compliance investigations
This policy governs evidence source selection for all OASIS data items at all assessment time points (SOC, ROC, RECERT, FU/SCIC, TRN, DC) and for all clinical documentation decisions where multiple evidence sources exist and must be prioritized. It does not alter the CMS OASIS-E2 Guidance Manual's item-specific instructions — where the Guidance Manual specifies a particular data collection method for a specific item, that specification governs. This policy establishes the framework that applies when the Guidance Manual does not specify a single source or when multiple applicable sources must be reconciled.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 All OASIS coding decisions at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. shall be grounded in evidence drawn from the highest available level of the Documentation Hierarchy defined in Section 5 of this policy. When evidence from a higher-level source is available and applicable, it shall govern the coding decision over evidence from a lower-level source.
4.2 No OASIS item response shall be selected on the basis of a lower-level evidence source when a higher-level source provides directly applicable clinical information for that item during the applicable look-back period.
4.3 When evidence sources conflict — that is, when a higher-level source and a lower-level source describe the patient's status differently for the same OASIS item — the assessor shall apply the evidence hierarchy per Section 5, document the conflicting sources in the assessment narrative, explain why the higher-level source was selected, and initiate the conflicting source reconciliation process per CL-OA-008 if the conflict has clinical implications beyond the immediate coding decision.
4.4 The evidence source used to support every OASIS coding decision shall be identifiable in the assessment narrative documentation. It is not sufficient to code an OASIS item accurately if the clinical record does not contain documentation that a reviewer or surveyor can use to verify the coding decision. An OASIS response that cannot be traced to a specific, documentable evidence source is an unsupported response, regardless of its clinical plausibility.
4.5 Financial considerations — including PDGM payment group optimization, episode management, or revenue targets — shall not influence evidence source selection. Selecting a lower-level evidence source because it produces a more favorable payment outcome, when a higher-level source is available and applicable, constitutes data manipulation and a potential violation of the False Claims Act. Any direction from revenue cycle personnel, management, or consultants to select evidence sources on the basis of payment optimization rather than clinical accuracy shall be reported to the Compliance Officer immediately per CO-CP-006.
4.6 The Documentation Hierarchy applies to all clinical documentation decisions, not exclusively to OASIS coding. When a clinician must choose between conflicting sources to document a clinical finding in a visit note, plan of care, or assessment narrative, the same hierarchy applies. Consistent application of the hierarchy across all documentation types reinforces the internal consistency of the clinical record.
4.7 The Director of Nursing shall incorporate evidence source documentation into the monthly OASIS quality audit per CL-OA-002, verifying that audited assessments contain traceable evidence references for high-risk item categories and that evidence source selection is consistent with this policy.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Evidence Source | Any document, observation, test result, or verbal report that provides clinical information relevant to an OASIS coding decision or a clinical documentation entry. |
| Documentation Hierarchy | The priority ranking system established by this policy that governs the relative weight assigned to different categories of evidence sources when making OASIS coding decisions and resolving source conflicts. |
| Direct Clinical Observation | The assessing RN's own first-hand observation of the patient performing an activity, exhibiting a symptom, or demonstrating a functional level during the assessment encounter. The highest-weight evidence source. |
| Physical Examination Finding | A clinical finding obtained through hands-on physical examination by the assessing RN during the assessment encounter — including auscultation, palpation, range of motion testing, strength testing, and neurological assessment. |
| Standardized Tool Administration | A validated assessment instrument administered by the assessing RN during the assessment encounter in strict accordance with the validated protocol — including BIMS, PHQ-2/PHQ-9, MAHC-10, and other CMS-required tools. |
| Patient Self-Report | Information provided verbally by the patient about their own symptoms, functional abilities, medication use, or history. A primary but subjective source that requires corroboration for OASIS items requiring objective verification. |
| Caregiver Report | Information provided verbally by a caregiver (family member, paid caregiver, or household member) about the patient's functional abilities, symptoms, or history. Treated as corroborative with patient self-report rather than as an independent primary source. |
| Internal Clinical Record | Documentation generated within the current Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. home health episode — including prior visit notes, prior assessments, physician communication notes, medication reconciliation records, and laboratory results obtained during the episode. |
| External Clinical Documentation | Documentation generated by healthcare providers or facilities outside Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. — including hospital discharge summaries, SNF discharge records, physician office notes, specialist reports, and prior home health agency records. |
| Inference | A coding decision based on logical extrapolation from available evidence rather than on direct clinical observation, patient report, or documented clinical findings. The lowest-weight evidence basis; requires explicit documentation of the inferential reasoning. |
| Evidence Traceability | The ability of a reviewer to identify, in the clinical record, the specific documentation or observation that supported a given OASIS coding decision. Required for all OASIS responses per Section 4.4. |

## 6. The Documentation Hierarchy — Evidence Source Priority Ranking
### 6.1 Hierarchy Structure
The following hierarchy governs evidence source selection at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. Sources are listed from highest priority (Level 1) to lowest priority (Level 6). When multiple sources are available, the highest applicable level governs.
LEVEL 1 — DIRECT CLINICAL OBSERVATION DURING THE ASSESSMENT ENCOUNTER (Highest Priority)
Definition: The assessing RN directly observes the patient performing the activity, demonstrating the functional level, or exhibiting the symptom being coded — during the current assessment visit, within the applicable look-back period.
Application: For GG functional items (GG0130, GG0170), Level 1 evidence is obtained by asking the patient to perform the activity during the visit and directly observing the performance — not by asking the patient or caregiver to describe what they can do. For wound assessment items (M1311–M1350), Level 1 evidence is obtained by undressing all wound dressings and directly observing wound status. For behavioral observation items (M1710, M1720, M1740), Level 1 evidence includes directly witnessing behavioral symptoms during the visit.
Documentation Standard: The visit note shall describe what the assessor directly observed — the specific activity, the level of assistance required, the qualitative characteristics of the performance, and any safety concerns identified. Documentation shall be specific enough that a second clinician reviewing the record could independently verify the observation.
Examples of Adequate Level 1 Documentation:
"Patient directly observed ambulating 25 feet in the hallway with rolling walker. Required standby assist for balance at the turn. Gait was slow, wide-based, and slightly unsteady but no loss of balance. Completed the distance in 48 seconds."
"Stage 2 pressure injury directly observed on the right heel — dressing removed for assessment. Wound measures 2.1 cm x 1.8 cm x 0.2 cm. Wound bed 80% granulation tissue, 20% yellow slough. Periwound skin is intact without maceration. No drainage. No odor."
Examples of Inadequate Level 1 Documentation:
"Patient ambulates with walker." (No observation detail; does not establish GG performance level)
"Wound healing well." (No objective wound assessment data)
LEVEL 2 — PHYSICAL EXAMINATION FINDINGS DURING THE ASSESSMENT ENCOUNTER
Definition: A clinical finding obtained through hands-on examination by the assessing RN during the current assessment visit — not observed activity performance, but assessed physical status.
Application: Applicable to items where the assessor performs an examination rather than observing activity performance. Examples include: lung auscultation findings for respiratory items; cardiac auscultation and peripheral edema palpation for cardiac items; skin turgor and mucous membrane assessment for hydration/nutritional items; neurological reflex testing; range of motion measurement; muscle strength grading; sensory testing (monofilament); blood pressure and vital signs measurement.
Documentation Standard: The examination finding shall be documented with the specific technique used, the specific finding obtained, and the specific anatomical location or measurement. A finding documented as "WNL" without supporting examination detail is inadequate.
Examples of Adequate Level 2 Documentation:
"Lung auscultation: bibasilar crackles present posterior fields bilaterally, approximately one-third of the way up from the bases. No wheezes. No pleural rub."
"Right lower extremity edema — pitting 2+ to mid-calf. Left lower extremity — trace non-pitting edema at ankle. Skin intact bilaterally, no breakdown."
"Active range of motion — right shoulder flexion to 95 degrees (limited by pain; patient reports 8/10 pain at endpoint). Strength — right deltoid 3+/5 per MMT."
LEVEL 3 — STANDARDIZED ASSESSMENT TOOL RESULTS FROM THE ASSESSMENT ENCOUNTER
Definition: Results from standardized assessment instruments administered by the assessing RN during the current assessment visit, in strict accordance with validated administration protocols.
Application: Applies specifically to CMS-required standardized tools — BIMS (for M1700), PHQ-2/PHQ-9 (for M1730/M1750), MAHC-10 (where applicable), and any other CMS-mandated tool for the current OASIS version. Also applies to validated discipline-specific tools used during the assessment (Timed Up and Go test, Berg Balance Scale, functional reach, etc.).
Documentation Standard: The specific tool name and version, all individual item scores, the total score, and the clinical interpretation of the score shall be documented. The administration conditions shall be noted — particularly any deviation from the standard protocol (patient fatigue, interpreter used, partial administration with reason). See CL-OA-011 for standardized tool administration requirements.
Critical Rule: A standardized tool score is only Level 3 evidence if the tool was administered in accordance with its validated protocol during the current assessment encounter. An abbreviated BIMS, a BIMS administered without the word repetition component, or a BIMS inferred from prior assessments does not constitute Level 3 evidence for the current assessment.
LEVEL 4 — PATIENT SELF-REPORT WITH CORROBORATION
Definition: Information provided verbally by the patient about their own symptoms, functional abilities, medication use, or history — when corroborated by at least one of: (a) physical examination findings; (b) caregiver report; (c) internal clinical record entries; or (d) external clinical documentation.
Application: Patient self-report is a primary evidence source for many OASIS items — particularly symptom items (pain, dyspnea, anxiety), activity items with look-back periods (where direct observation of the activity at the assessment is not feasible), and history items. However, self-report alone is not sufficient for items where objective verification is clinically feasible and required by the CMS Guidance Manual.
Uncorroborated Patient Self-Report: When a patient self-report cannot be corroborated — for example, a patient reports they are fully independent in ambulation, but no direct observation is performed and no corroborating source is available — the assessor shall document the report, note the absence of corroboration, and explain the clinical reason why direct observation was not performed. Uncorroborated self-report for items where objective verification is feasible constitutes Level 5 evidence (single source report), not Level 4.
Documentation Standard: The specific patient statement, the corroborating source, and the reconciliation of any inconsistency between the patient report and the corroborating source shall be documented.
LEVEL 5 — SINGLE-SOURCE REPORTS (CAREGIVER REPORT / UNCORROBORATED PATIENT SELF-REPORT / INTERNAL CLINICAL RECORD)
Definition: Information from a single source that cannot be corroborated by another independent source during the current assessment. This includes: caregiver-only reports (no corresponding patient confirmation or clinical examination finding); uncorroborated patient self-report for items where corroboration is feasible; and internal clinical record entries from prior visits during the current episode, when no direct observation at the current assessment is possible.
Application and Limitations: Level 5 sources are appropriate when Level 1–4 sources are not available or applicable — for example, when a patient lacks the communication capacity to self-report and no direct observation is possible, the caregiver's report of the patient's typical functional status is the best available evidence. Level 5 sources are also appropriate as the primary evidence for items with extended look-back periods, where the look-back extends beyond what the assessor can directly observe during a single visit.
Caregiver Report Caution: Caregiver reports may reflect the caregiver's capabilities and preferences rather than the patient's actual abilities. A caregiver who routinely performs all ADLs for the patient may report the patient as "unable to do anything" even if the patient retains residual abilities. The assessor must probe for the patient's actual typical performance, not the caregiver's typical assistance level. When caregiver report and clinical examination findings conflict, the clinical examination governs (Level 2 over Level 5).
Documentation Standard: The specific source, the information provided, and any limitations or qualifications of the source shall be documented. If Level 5 evidence is used for a GG functional item where direct observation is normally expected, the reason direct observation was not performed shall be documented.
LEVEL 6 — EXTERNAL CLINICAL DOCUMENTATION AND INFERENCE (Lowest Priority for Current Assessment Status)
Definition:
External clinical documentation: Records generated by providers outside Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. during a prior care episode or concurrent care encounter — including hospital discharge summaries, SNF records, physician office notes, specialist reports, and prior home health agency records.
Inference: A coding decision based on logical extrapolation from available evidence when no direct evidence is available for the specific item — for example, inferring a patient's pain level from behavioral observations when the patient cannot self-report.
Application — External Documentation: External documentation is appropriately used for: history items (diagnoses, surgical history, hospitalization history); medication list verification (cross-checked against the patient's actual medication bottles as Level 1/2 verification); establishing the patient's baseline prior to the current episode; and identifying clinical conditions documented by prior treating providers that the current assessor cannot independently verify.
External documentation is not appropriate as the primary basis for OASIS items that reflect the patient's current functional status, unless the external document is contemporaneous with the current assessment time point and from a qualified clinical provider who directly assessed the patient.
Critical Warning: Coding a patient's current GG functional status based on a hospital discharge summary's functional description, without direct observation at the SOC visit, is a Level 6 coding decision for a Level 1 item. This is the most common evidence hierarchy violation identified in ADR audits. The hospital's functional status description at discharge represents the patient's status at discharge — it does not represent the patient's status at the home health SOC, which may be better, worse, or the same.
Inference Application: When inference is the only available basis for a coding decision (patient is comatose; patient refuses assessment; patient is transferred and not present for the TRN assessment), the assessor shall document: the specific clinical evidence available; the inferential reasoning applied; and the confidence level in the inferred response. Inference-based responses shall be flagged for OASIS Quality Reviewer review per CL-OA-002.
Documentation Standard for Inference: "Direct observation of [specific activity] was not possible because [specific reason]. The available evidence — [description of available evidence] — supports a coding response of [response]. Reasoning: [specific clinical reasoning]."
### 6.2 Evidence Hierarchy Application by OASIS Item Category

| OASIS Item Category | Primary Evidence Level | Secondary Evidence Level | Common Error |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| GG Functional Items (GG0130, GG0170) | Level 1 — Direct observation of the patient performing the activity during the visit | Level 4 — Patient self-report with corroboration, for items not feasibly observed | Coding from hospital discharge summary (Level 6) without direct observation |
| Wound Items (M1311–M1350) | Level 1 — Direct observation of wound after dressing removal | Level 2 — Physical examination of periwound tissue | Coding from prior visit note without observing the wound at the current assessment |
| Behavioral Health Items (M1700 — BIMS) | Level 3 — BIMS administration during assessment | Level 5 — SAMS (staff assessment) if BIMS cannot be administered | Abbreviated BIMS or BIMS inferred from prior assessment |
| Behavioral Health Items (M1730 — PHQ-2/PHQ-9) | Level 3 — PHQ-2/PHQ-9 administration during assessment | Level 1 — Direct observation of depressive behaviors if patient cannot complete tool | Coding M1730 from clinical impression without tool administration |
| Medication Items (M2001, M2003, M2010) | Level 2 — Medication review conducted during visit with physical inventory | Level 4 — Patient self-report of medication use | Coding from the medication list alone without patient interview and bottle review |
| Respiratory Items | Level 2 — Lung auscultation and vital signs during visit | Level 1 — Direct observation of respiratory effort and accessory muscle use | Coding SpO2 without documentation of liter flow and delivery device |
| Cardiac / Circulation Items | Level 2 — Physical examination (auscultation, edema palpation, peripheral pulses) | Level 1 — Direct observation of functional limitations during assessment | Coding edema from prior visit note without current examination |
| Homebound Status | Level 1 and 2 — Observed functional limitations and physical examination findings during the assessment encounter | Level 4 — Patient self-report of limitations | Copying homebound language from SOC to RECERT without re-assessment |
| History Items (diagnoses, surgery, hospitalization) | Level 6 — External clinical documentation (discharge summary, physician records) | Level 4 — Patient self-report of history | Accepting a referral's diagnosis without verifying against assessment findings |
| Nutritional Items | Level 2 — Physical examination (weight, skin, mucous membranes) | Level 4 — Patient/caregiver report of intake | Coding nutritional status without documenting a weight measurement |

## 7. Procedures
### 7.1 Evidence Collection During Assessment Visits

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7.1.1 | Assessing RN | Before beginning the OASIS assessment, review all available pre-visit documentation (referral records, prior notes, medication lists) to identify the items that will be assessed and to plan the observation and examination sequence that will generate the highest-level evidence for each applicable item. Do not pre-populate any OASIS response based on pre-visit documentation alone — this is a Level 6 evidence basis for items that require Level 1 or 2 evidence. | Before each assessment visit. |
| 7.1.2 | Assessing RN | During the assessment visit, structure the clinical encounter to generate direct observation and physical examination evidence for all GG functional items and examination-dependent items. This means asking the patient to perform activities rather than asking whether they can perform them; removing wound dressings to directly observe all wounds; conducting a full physical examination including auscultation, palpation, and neurological assessment as appropriate to the diagnoses; and administering all required standardized tools in validated protocol. | During the assessment visit. |
| 7.1.3 | Assessing RN | When direct observation of a specific activity is clinically unsafe, practically impossible, or refused by the patient, document the reason and note the evidence level being used as the substitute. Notify the Director of Nursing if the inability to obtain Level 1 or 2 evidence affects a high-risk OASIS item (GG items, wound items). | At the time of the assessment; notification within 24 hours. |
| 7.1.4 | Assessing RN | After completing the assessment visit, complete the narrative documentation before coding the OASIS responses. The narrative shall precede the OASIS responses — do not reverse-engineer narrative to match OASIS responses that were pre-populated from external sources. | Within the required documentation timeframe per CL-OA-001. |

### 7.2 Documentation of Evidence Sources in the Assessment Narrative

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7.2.1 | Assessing RN | For each OASIS item being coded, the assessment narrative shall contain documentation that a reviewer can use to verify the evidentiary basis. For Level 1 items (direct observation), this means describing what was observed in specific, objective terms. For Level 2 items (physical examination), this means documenting the specific examination finding. For Level 3 items (standardized tools), this means documenting the individual item scores and total score. For Level 4-6 items, this means documenting the source, the information provided, and any corroborating or conflicting information. | In the assessment narrative; concurrent with or before OASIS coding. |
| 7.2.2 | Assessing RN | When using Level 5 or 6 evidence for an item where higher-level evidence would normally be expected — for example, coding a GG item from caregiver report because the patient refused to perform the activity — include the specific notation: "Level [X] evidence used for [OASIS item] because [specific reason higher-level evidence was not available]. Evidence basis: [description of evidence]." | In the assessment narrative. |
| 7.2.3 | Assessing RN | Never document an evidence source that was not actually used. If the wound assessment was done from a prior note (Level 6) rather than direct wound observation (Level 1), do not document a wound description in language suggesting direct observation occurred. This constitutes falsification of medical records regardless of whether the coded OASIS response happens to be accurate. | At all times. |

### 7.3 Quality Review Integration

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 7.3.1 | OASIS Quality Reviewer | During each Level 2 quality review per CL-OA-002, specifically assess evidence traceability for all GG functional items and wound items in the reviewed assessment. For each reviewed item, verify: (a) the narrative contains documentation at the appropriate evidence level; (b) the coded OASIS response is consistent with the documented evidence; (c) no lower-level evidence source was used when higher-level evidence was documented in the narrative. | Within the timeline specified in CL-OA-002. |
| 7.3.2 | Director of Nursing | During monthly OASIS accuracy audits per CL-OA-002, include evidence traceability as a specific audit category. Calculate the percentage of audited assessments where every reviewed OASIS item has traceable, appropriate-level evidence documentation. Report this as a separate metric in the OASIS Accuracy Dashboard. | Monthly. |
| 7.3.3 | Director of Nursing | When an audited assessment reveals Level 6 evidence used for GG functional items without documented clinical justification, treat this as a Priority 1 finding requiring individual coaching within 7 calendar days and targeted retraining within 14 calendar days. Report the finding to the Compliance Officer if the pattern appears across multiple assessors or assessments. | Coaching within 7 calendar days; Compliance Officer notification for patterns. |

## 8. Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Assessor is instructed by revenue cycle or management to select a lower-level evidence source to achieve a higher PDGM payment group | Assessor immediately contacts Compliance Officer | Compliance Officer investigates per CO-CP-007. All assessments completed under the instruction are reviewed for accuracy. If financially motivated coding decisions are confirmed, assess for False Claims Act exposure per CO-FA-002 and initiate voluntary correction per FN-BC-004 if overpayment occurred. | Compliance Officer contact immediately; investigation within 24 hours; correction assessment within 14 calendar days. |
| An assessment is identified where GG functional items were coded from the hospital discharge summary without SOC direct observation | Director of Nursing and OASIS Quality Reviewer | Conduct direct clinical observation at the next scheduled visit. If the observation reveals functional status materially different from the coded OASIS response, correct the assessment per CL-OA-002. Assess payment impact with Compliance Officer. Provide targeted coaching to the assessor. | Re-observation at next visit; correction determination within 5 business days of re-observation. |
| A patient refuses to perform any activities during the assessment, making Level 1 evidence collection impossible for all GG items | Assessing RN documents refusal; Director of Nursing notified | Director of Nursing provides guidance on use of caregiver report and clinical observation (Level 5) for the current assessment. Increase visit frequency to obtain Level 1 evidence at the next available visit. Document the clinical circumstances thoroughly. | Documentation at assessment; Director of Nursing guidance within 24 hours. |
| Evidence sources conflict across all six hierarchy levels — no single source clearly governs | Assessing RN and Director of Nursing | Apply the evidence hierarchy in sequence. If the conflict cannot be resolved, use the clinical judgment documentation process per CL-OA-012. Escalate to the OASIS Quality Reviewer for a pre-lock review of the affected items. | Pre-lock review within 5 business days. |

## 9. Documentation Requirements

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Evidence-level documentation for all GG functional items | Assessment narrative with specific observation descriptions per Level 1 standards | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment module and visit note | Concurrent with OASIS completion; retained minimum 7 years |
| Evidence-level documentation for all wound items | Direct wound observation documentation per Level 1 and 2 standards | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment module; Wound documentation module | At each applicable time point; retained minimum 7 years |
| Standardized tool results with item-level scores | PHQ-2/PHQ-9, BIMS, MAHC-10 (as applicable) with each component score | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment module | At each applicable time point; retained minimum 7 years |
| Level 5 or 6 evidence notation | Explicit documentation of evidence level and reason when lower-level sources are used | Assessing RN | EHR — Assessment narrative | At the time of each such use; retained minimum 7 years |
| Monthly evidence traceability audit results | Audit findings including evidence traceability metric | Director of Nursing | OASIS Accuracy Dashboard; Director of Nursing supervisory file | Monthly; retained minimum 7 years |
| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment — Appendix A | Each individual; Administrator (collection) | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days of effective date, revision, or hire |

## 10. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 10.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| GG functional items coded from Level 1 direct observation when the patient was present and capable | Monthly OASIS audit — cross-reference GG responses with assessment narrative observation documentation | ≥95% of GG items with documented direct observation or clinically justified exception |
| Wound items coded from direct wound observation | Monthly OASIS audit — verify narrative contains wound description at Level 1 standard | ≥98% of wound items coded from direct observation at the assessment encounter |
| Standardized tool scores documented at item level | Monthly audit of BIMS and PHQ-2/PHQ-9 documentation | ≥98% of tool administrations with item-level scores documented |
| Level 5/6 evidence uses documented with explicit notation | Audit of assessments where Level 5/6 evidence was the primary source | ≥95% of Level 5/6 uses with explicit evidence level notation |
| No evidence of revenue-motivated source selection | Compliance Officer quarterly review of coding patterns | Zero confirmed instances |

### 10.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS OASIS validation surveyors will independently assess patients in the survey sample and compare their clinical findings to the submitted OASIS data. The most common discrepancy they identify — and the one most directly linked to evidence hierarchy violations — is GG functional items coded at a higher level of dependence than the patient's direct performance demonstrates. When a surveyor observes a patient ambulate 100 feet independently with a cane and the submitted OASIS shows "Substantial/Maximal Assistance" for walking, the inevitable conclusion is that the coding was not based on direct observation. Surveyors will ask the assessing RN to describe the evidence basis for the GG responses. If the assessor cannot identify a specific direct observation or examination finding — and the narrative does not document one — the assessment will be cited as inaccurate.
ADR auditors from the MAC will specifically examine assessment narratives for the presence of specific, objective clinical descriptions that corroborate OASIS responses. A narrative that says "patient requires assistance with mobility" without describing what was observed does not adequately support a specific GG functional item response. Auditors are trained to recognize when narratives have been copied from external sources (hospital discharge language appearing in the SOC narrative) or when the narrative descriptions are generic and non-specific.
### 10.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| SOC GG items coded from hospital discharge functional description without SOC direct observation | ADR denial; OASIS inaccuracy; potential upcoding | Train all assessors on the non-transferability of discharge status to SOC status; require GG observation documentation in EHR before OASIS can be locked |
| Wound items coded from prior visit notes at RECERT without current wound observation | OASIS inaccuracy at RECERT; quality measure distortion | Include wound observation confirmation as mandatory pre-lock checklist item per CL-OA-019 |
| BIMS coded from clinical impression rather than formal tool administration | M1700 inaccuracy; behavioral health PDGM classification error | Annual BIMS competency demonstration required; OASIS Quality Reviewer verifies item-level score documentation |
| Assessment narrative describes patient performing activity but GG response does not reflect the described performance | Internal inconsistency between Level 1 observation and OASIS coding | Director of Nursing monthly audit includes narrative-to-GG cross-reference as a required audit step |
