# CL-SD-014 — Pain Assessment & Management
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-SD-014 |
| Policy Title | Pain Assessment & Management |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | SD — Service Delivery |
| Classification Tier | REQUIRED |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

## 2. Purpose
This policy defines the requirements for pain screening, assessment, reassessment, and individualized pain management planning for all patients served by Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. Pain is a subjective experience that significantly affects the patient's functional status, quality of life, participation in rehabilitation, medication adherence, sleep, appetite, and overall recovery trajectory. Inadequate pain assessment is a patient safety failure; inadequate pain management is a clinical quality failure. Conversely, over-reliance on opioid analgesics without a comprehensive pain management approach contributes to the national opioid crisis and requires vigilant clinical oversight. This policy ensures that pain is assessed at every patient encounter using validated tools, that pain management is individualized and multimodal, and that all pain-related clinical activities are documented in compliance with 42 CFR § 484.60, CMS OASIS pain item requirements, and evidence-based clinical practice guidelines.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all clinical disciplines (RN, LVN, PT, OT, SLP, MSW, HHA) — as each discipline has a role in pain identification, assessment, and/or management within their scope. Specifically: RNs conduct comprehensive pain assessments and manage pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic interventions; LVNs conduct focused pain assessments and administer pain medications; PTs, OTs, and SLPs assess pain within the context of their therapeutic interventions; MSWs assess psychosocial aspects of pain; HHAs observe and report pain indicators.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Pain shall be screened at every patient encounter by every clinical discipline — using a validated, age-appropriate, and cognitively appropriate pain screening tool. Pain is the "fifth vital sign" and shall be documented with the same rigor and consistency as blood pressure, pulse, temperature, and respiration.
4.2 At SOC and at each OASIS assessment time point, the assigned RN shall conduct a comprehensive pain assessment including: (a) pain location(s); (b) pain intensity using a validated scale; (c) pain quality (sharp, dull, burning, aching, throbbing, stabbing); (d) pain onset, duration, and pattern (constant, intermittent, activity-related); (e) aggravating and alleviating factors; (f) impact of pain on function (mobility, ADLs, sleep, appetite, mood); (g) current pain management strategies — both pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic; (h) patient's pain management goals; (i) assessment for risk factors for opioid misuse (if applicable) per RM-PS-005.
4.3 Pain management shall be multimodal — incorporating pharmacologic interventions (per physician order), non-pharmacologic interventions (positioning, heat/cold therapy, relaxation techniques, guided imagery, therapeutic exercise), and patient education on self-management strategies.
4.4 Pain reassessment shall be conducted: (a) at every skilled visit; (b) within 1 hour of any pain medication administration during a visit; (c) following any non-pharmacologic pain intervention; (d) whenever the patient reports a change in pain pattern, intensity, or location.
4.5 All OASIS pain items shall be coded accurately and consistently with the narrative pain assessment documentation in the visit note per CL-OA-007.
4.6 The physician shall be notified within 24 hours when: (a) the patient's pain is uncontrolled despite current interventions; (b) a change in pain medication is indicated; (c) the patient reports new pain or a significant change in existing pain; (d) the patient is exhibiting signs of opioid adverse effects (sedation, respiratory depression, constipation, confusion).
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Pain Screening | A brief, standardized assessment to identify the presence and intensity of pain, typically using a single numeric or descriptive scale. |
| Comprehensive Pain Assessment | A thorough, multidimensional assessment of the patient's pain experience including location, intensity, quality, pattern, impact on function, and management effectiveness. |
| Numeric Rating Scale (NRS) | A validated self-report pain scale where the patient rates pain intensity from 0 (no pain) to 10 (worst possible pain). |
| Wong-Baker FACES Scale | A validated pain assessment tool using facial expressions to indicate pain intensity — appropriate for patients with communication or cognitive limitations. |
| FLACC Scale | A behavioral pain assessment tool (Face, Legs, Activity, Cry, Consolability) used for patients who are unable to self-report, including patients with severe cognitive impairment. |
| Multimodal Pain Management | An approach combining pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic interventions to address pain through multiple mechanisms. |
| Breakthrough Pain | Pain that occurs despite the use of regular scheduled pain medication, requiring additional "as needed" (PRN) analgesic dosing. |
| Non-Pharmacologic Intervention | A pain management technique that does not involve medications, including positioning, heat/cold application, massage, relaxation, guided imagery, distraction, and therapeutic exercise. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Pain Screening at Every Visit

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | All Clinical Disciplines | At every patient encounter, screen for pain by asking the patient: "Are you experiencing any pain right now?" and "Have you had pain since my last visit?" If the patient is unable to self-report, use behavioral observation per Section 6.1.3. | At every visit. |
| 6.1.2 | All Clinical Disciplines | If the patient reports pain, assess intensity using the appropriate validated tool: (a) Numeric Rating Scale (NRS, 0–10) for patients who can self-report; (b) Wong-Baker FACES Scale for patients who prefer a visual scale or have mild cognitive limitations; (c) FLACC Scale for patients unable to self-report. Document the tool used and the score. | At every visit where pain is reported. |
| 6.1.3 | RN / LVN | For patients unable to self-report pain (severe cognitive impairment, aphasia, advanced dementia), observe for behavioral pain indicators: facial grimacing, guarding, moaning, agitation, restlessness, resistance to care, changes in vital signs. Apply the FLACC scale or equivalent validated behavioral tool. Document the behavioral assessment. | At every visit for non-verbal patients. |

### 6.2 Comprehensive Pain Assessment at SOC and OASIS Time Points

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assigned RN | At SOC and at each OASIS assessment time point, conduct a comprehensive pain assessment per Section 4.2. Document all elements in the clinical record using the Pain Assessment Documentation Template (Appendix A). | At SOC and each OASIS time point. |
| 6.2.2 | Assigned RN | Develop a pain management plan as part of the plan of care, including: (a) the patient's stated pain management goal (e.g., "pain at 4/10 or below with activity"); (b) scheduled and PRN pharmacologic interventions ordered by the physician; (c) non-pharmacologic interventions appropriate to the patient's condition; (d) patient education on pain self-management strategies. | At SOC; updated at each reassessment. |
| 6.2.3 | Assigned RN | Ensure OASIS pain items are coded accurately and are consistent with the narrative pain assessment per CL-OA-007. | At each OASIS time point. |

### 6.3 Pain Reassessment and Intervention Monitoring

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN / LVN | At each skilled visit, reassess pain and document: (a) current pain intensity using the same tool as prior assessments; (b) comparison to prior visit; (c) effectiveness of current pain management; (d) patient's adherence to the pain management plan; (e) any new pain or change in existing pain. | At each visit. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN / LVN | If a pain medication is administered during the visit, reassess and document the patient's pain intensity within 1 hour of administration (or within the expected onset time of the medication) to evaluate effectiveness. | Within 1 hour of medication administration. |
| 6.3.3 | Assigned RN / LVN | If the patient's pain is not adequately controlled (exceeds the patient's stated goal or is ≥7/10), implement available non-pharmacologic interventions and notify the physician within 24 hours to request a medication or treatment plan adjustment. | Interventions immediately; physician notification within 24 hours. |

### 6.4 Opioid-Specific Monitoring

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Assigned RN | For patients receiving opioid analgesics, assess at each visit: (a) pain control effectiveness; (b) sedation level using the Pasero Opioid-Induced Sedation Scale (POSS) or equivalent; (c) respiratory rate and depth; (d) bowel function (opioid-induced constipation); (e) functional impact of opioids; (f) signs of misuse or diversion per RM-PS-005. | At each visit for opioid patients. |
| 6.4.2 | Assigned RN | Notify the physician immediately if the patient exhibits: (a) respiratory rate <12/min; (b) excessive sedation (POSS ≥3); (c) signs of opioid overdose. If overdose is suspected, call 911 immediately and administer naloxone if available per physician standing order. | Immediately. |

### 6.5 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Uncontrolled pain despite current regimen (pain ≥7/10 for 2 consecutive visits) | Assigned RN notifies physician and Director of Nursing | Physician adjusts medication regimen. Director of Nursing reviews pain management plan and considers specialist referral (pain management, palliative care). Document all actions. | Physician notification within 24 hours; Director of Nursing review within 48 hours. |
| Patient requests opioid dose escalation beyond physician parameters | Assigned RN notifies physician | Physician evaluates the request. RN documents the patient's request, the physician's response, and the clinical rationale. | Physician notification within 24 hours. |
| Suspected opioid misuse or diversion | RN notifies Director of Nursing and Compliance Officer | Follow RM-PS-005 and CO-FA-003 protocols. Physician notification. Assessment of alternative pain management strategies. | Director of Nursing within 24 hours; Compliance Officer within 48 hours. |
| Pain assessment not documented at a skilled visit | Director of Nursing identifies during chart review | Director of Nursing provides corrective coaching. Clinician completes a late-entry pain assessment per CO-DC-003 if clinically possible. | Coaching within 7 calendar days. |

## 7. Documentation Requirements

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pain screening at every visit | Pain score and tool used documented in visit note | All clinical disciplines | EHR — visit note | At each visit; within 24 hours |
| Comprehensive pain assessment at SOC/OASIS | Completed Pain Assessment Documentation Template (Appendix A) | Assigned RN | EHR — assessment module | At SOC and OASIS time points |
| Pain management plan | Documented in the plan of care | Assigned RN | EHR — plan of care | At SOC; updated as needed |
| Post-intervention reassessment | Pain score after medication administration or non-pharmacologic intervention | Assigned RN / LVN | EHR — visit note | Within 1 hour of intervention |
| Opioid monitoring | Sedation scale, respiratory rate, bowel function, functional assessment | Assigned RN | EHR — visit note | At each visit for opioid patients |
| Physician notifications for pain concerns | Communication documentation | Assigned RN | EHR — communication notes | Within 24 hours; immediately for urgent concerns |
| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment (Appendix B) | Each individual; Administrator (collection) | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pain screening documented at every skilled visit | Monthly chart audit | ≥95% of audited visits include pain screening |
| Comprehensive pain assessment at SOC | SOC chart audit | ≥95% with all required elements documented |
| Post-medication pain reassessment documented | Chart audit for visits with pain medication administration | ≥90% with documented reassessment |
| OASIS pain items consistent with narrative assessment | OASIS-to-narrative cross-reference audit | ≥95% consistency |
| Uncontrolled pain results in physician notification | Audit of communication notes for patients with pain scores ≥7 | ≥95% with documented physician notification |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors will verify that pain assessment is a component of every skilled visit, that validated tools are used, that pain management is individualized and not solely pharmacologic, and that there is evidence of reassessment following interventions. Surveyors may interview patients about their pain experience and whether staff asked about their pain. Failure to assess pain at every visit is a commonly cited deficiency.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pain documented as a number only (e.g., "pain 5/10") without context | Incomplete assessment; survey deficiency | Require pain location, quality, and impact documentation at minimum |
| Same pain score documented at every visit without clinical analysis | Suggests assessment is not being performed | Train clinicians to analyze trends and document comparison to prior visits |
| Non-pharmacologic interventions not offered or documented | Over-reliance on medications; survey citation for non-comprehensive approach | Include non-pharmacologic intervention checklist in visit note template |
| Opioid monitoring not documented for patients on opioids | Patient safety risk; regulatory concern | EHR alert for opioid patients requiring enhanced monitoring documentation |

# CL-SD-015 — Fall Risk Assessment & Prevention
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-SD-015 |
| Policy Title | Fall Risk Assessment & Prevention |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | SD — Service Delivery |
| Classification Tier | REQUIRED |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the fall risk screening, assessment, intervention planning, and documentation requirements for all patients served by Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. Falls are the leading cause of injury-related death and hospitalization among older adults, and fall prevention is a core quality measure in home health. Falls in the home health population are tracked through OASIS-derived quality measures and are publicly reported on CMS Home Health Compare. A fall resulting in hospitalization or major injury during the home health episode is an adverse event that directly impacts the agency's quality scores, star ratings, and survey outcomes. This policy ensures that every patient receives a standardized fall risk assessment at admission and at defined intervals, that individualized fall prevention interventions are implemented and documented, that falls are reported and investigated, and that fall prevention education is provided to every patient and caregiver.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all clinical disciplines (RN, LVN, PT, OT, SLP, MSW, HHA), as every clinician has a role in fall risk identification and prevention. PTs and OTs have primary responsibility for functional mobility and balance assessment; RNs have primary responsibility for medication-related fall risk assessment and comprehensive risk factor identification; all disciplines are responsible for environmental safety assessment and patient education.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Fall risk screening shall be performed at every patient encounter by every clinical discipline — if a patient reports a fall or near-fall since the last visit, or if the clinician observes any change in the patient's mobility, balance, or cognitive status, a comprehensive fall risk reassessment shall be initiated.
4.2 A comprehensive fall risk assessment shall be completed by the assigned RN at SOC, at each OASIS assessment time point, following any fall, and whenever a significant change in the patient's condition affects fall risk. The assessment shall use a validated fall risk assessment tool (e.g., Morse Fall Scale, Timed Up and Go test, or equivalent) and shall include all risk factors identified in Section 6.2.
4.3 An individualized Fall Prevention Plan shall be developed as part of the plan of care for every patient identified as at-risk for falls. The plan shall address modifiable risk factors and shall be reviewed and updated at each recertification and following any fall.
4.4 All falls occurring during the home health episode — whether witnessed by agency staff, reported by the patient/caregiver, or identified through clinical assessment — shall be documented, reported to the physician within 24 hours, assessed for injury, and reported through the agency's incident reporting system per RM-ER-002 and adverse event reporting per QA-AE-001.
4.5 Fall prevention education shall be provided to the patient and caregiver at SOC and reinforced at each visit, including: personal risk factors, home safety modifications, safe transfer and ambulation techniques, appropriate footwear, medication-related fall risk, and when to call for assistance.
4.6 OASIS fall-related items shall be coded accurately and consistently with the clinical record per CL-OA-007.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Fall | An unplanned descent to the floor (or extension of the floor, e.g., a step or stool), with or without injury, whether or not caused by a physiological condition. |
| Near-Fall | An event where the patient begins to fall but recovers without fully descending to the floor, or is caught by a caregiver or assistive device. |
| Fall Risk Assessment | A standardized evaluation of factors that increase a patient's likelihood of falling, using a validated tool and clinical judgment. |
| Modifiable Risk Factor | A fall risk factor that can be changed or mitigated through clinical intervention — including medication adjustment, vision correction, assistive device use, home modification, strength training, and balance training. |
| Non-Modifiable Risk Factor | A fall risk factor that cannot be changed — including age, history of prior falls, certain neurological diagnoses, and cognitive impairment. |
| Fall Prevention Plan | An individualized plan of interventions designed to reduce the patient's fall risk, incorporated into the plan of care. |
| Environmental Safety Assessment | An assessment of the patient's home environment for fall hazards including loose rugs, poor lighting, cluttered walkways, wet floors, lack of grab bars, and stairs without handrails. Governed by RM-PS-001. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Fall Risk Screening at Every Visit

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | All Clinical Disciplines | At every patient visit, ask the patient/caregiver: "Have you fallen or almost fallen since my last visit?" and "Do you feel unsteady when standing or walking?" Document the response. | At every visit. |
| 6.1.2 | All Clinical Disciplines | Observe the patient's mobility during the visit — gait, balance, transfer ability, use of assistive devices. If any new instability, unsteadiness, or decline in mobility is observed, notify the assigned RN within 24 hours for fall risk reassessment. | At every visit. |

### 6.2 Comprehensive Fall Risk Assessment

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assigned RN | At SOC and at each OASIS time point, conduct a comprehensive fall risk assessment including: (a) history of falls in the past 12 months (number, circumstances, injuries); (b) current medications — review for fall-risk-increasing drugs (FRIDs): sedatives/hypnotics, opioids, antihypertensives, diuretics, antidepressants, anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, polypharmacy ≥5 medications; (c) gait and balance assessment using a validated tool (Timed Up and Go ≥12 seconds = increased risk; or Morse Fall Scale); (d) lower extremity strength assessment; (e) vision assessment — last eye exam, current visual acuity, corrective lens use; (f) cognitive status — impaired judgment, wandering risk per RM-PS-004; (g) orthostatic hypotension screening (blood pressure lying, sitting, standing); (h) environmental safety assessment per RM-PS-001; (i) continence status — urgency, frequency, nocturia; (j) footwear assessment; (k) assistive device use and condition. | At SOC and each OASIS time point; within 24 hours of any fall during the episode. |
| 6.2.2 | Assigned RN | Score and document the fall risk level using the agency's validated tool. Classify the patient as: Low Risk, Moderate Risk, or High Risk. | At the time of assessment. |
| 6.2.3 | PT / OT (if involved) | If PT or OT is involved in the patient's care, conduct a discipline-specific fall risk and functional mobility assessment using standardized tools (Berg Balance Scale, 30-Second Chair Stand, Single Leg Stance, Functional Reach Test). Communicate findings to the assigned RN for integration into the Fall Prevention Plan. | Within 48 hours of the initial therapy evaluation. |

### 6.3 Fall Prevention Plan Development

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN | For every patient identified as Moderate or High fall risk, develop an individualized Fall Prevention Plan as part of the plan of care, addressing each modifiable risk factor identified. Interventions shall include, as applicable: (a) medication review with physician — request review of FRIDs; (b) PT/OT referral for balance and strength training; (c) home safety modifications (remove loose rugs, improve lighting, install grab bars, clear walkways); (d) assistive device assessment, training, and proper use education; (e) orthostatic hypotension management; (f) vision referral if indicated; (g) continence management; (h) safe footwear education; (i) fall alert system recommendation; (j) patient and caregiver education. | Within 24 hours of the fall risk assessment. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN | Communicate the Fall Prevention Plan to all disciplines involved in the patient's care per CL-CP-005. | Within 48 hours. |
| 6.3.3 | Assigned RN | Review and update the Fall Prevention Plan at each recertification, following any fall, and whenever the patient's risk factors change. | At each recertification and after any fall. |

### 6.4 Fall Reporting and Post-Fall Assessment

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Any Clinician / HHA | When a fall is witnessed or reported during a visit, immediately assess the patient for injury: (a) level of consciousness; (b) vital signs; (c) visible injuries (lacerations, contusions, deformity suggesting fracture); (d) pain; (e) neurological status (if head injury is suspected). | Immediately upon discovery. |
| 6.4.2 | Any Clinician | If the patient has sustained a potential serious injury (suspected fracture, head injury, loss of consciousness, significant bleeding), call 911 immediately and notify the Director of Nursing within 2 hours. | 911 immediately; Director of Nursing within 2 hours. |
| 6.4.3 | Assigned RN | Notify the physician within 24 hours of any patient fall, regardless of injury severity. Obtain orders for any needed diagnostic evaluation (X-ray, CT) or treatment. | Within 24 hours. |
| 6.4.4 | Assigned RN | Complete an incident report per RM-ER-002 and an adverse event report per QA-AE-001 for every patient fall. | Within 24 hours. |
| 6.4.5 | Assigned RN | Conduct a post-fall assessment to determine the circumstances and contributing factors: (a) what was the patient doing at the time of the fall? (b) what was the mechanism (tripped, lost balance, legs gave way, dizziness)? (c) were assistive devices in use? (d) was medication a contributing factor? (e) were environmental hazards present? Document all findings. | Within 24 hours of the fall. |
| 6.4.6 | Assigned RN | Update the Fall Prevention Plan based on the post-fall assessment findings. If new modifiable risk factors are identified, implement targeted interventions. | Within 48 hours of the fall. |

### 6.5 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Patient falls twice or more during the episode | Director of Nursing is automatically notified | Director of Nursing conducts a case-level fall prevention review, including plan of care adequacy, medication review, home environment review, and PT/OT involvement. Recommends intensified interventions. | Director of Nursing review within 48 hours of second fall. |
| Patient refuses fall prevention interventions (refuses assistive device, refuses to remove rugs) | Assigned RN documents refusal; educates on risks | Notify physician. Document patient's informed refusal. Continue to educate at each visit. | Physician notification within 24 hours. |
| Fall results in hospitalization | Director of Nursing and QAPI Coordinator | Root cause analysis per QA-AE-002. QAPI review for systemic issues. | Root cause analysis within 7 calendar days. |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Fall risk screening at every skilled visit | Monthly chart audit | ≥95% |
| Comprehensive assessment at SOC with validated tool | SOC chart audit | ≥95% |
| Individualized Fall Prevention Plan for moderate/high risk patients | Plan of care audit | ≥95% |
| All falls reported through incident reporting | Cross-reference visit notes documenting falls with incident reports | 100% |
| Post-fall assessment completed within 24 hours | Post-fall documentation audit | ≥95% |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors will verify that fall risk is assessed at admission using a validated tool, that a fall prevention plan exists for at-risk patients, that falls are documented and reported, and that the agency tracks falls as a quality measure. Home Health Compare publicly reports the fall rate — a high fall rate damages the agency's star rating and public profile.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fall risk assessment performed but no Fall Prevention Plan developed | Survey deficiency; quality measure failure | EHR workflow requiring Fall Prevention Plan for moderate/high risk patients |
| Falls reported by patient but not documented or investigated | Underreporting; inability to demonstrate quality improvement | Train all disciplines to document reported falls; mandatory incident report for every fall |
| Environmental hazards identified but not addressed | Preventable falls; liability | Standardized home safety assessment per RM-PS-001 with documented interventions |
| Medication-related fall risk not assessed | Modifiable risk factor missed | Include FRID review in every fall risk assessment; pharmacist consultation for polypharmacy |

# CL-SD-016 — Infection Prevention & Control
## 1. Policy Header

## 2. Purpose
This policy defines the agency's infection prevention and control (IPC) program, including standard precautions, transmission-based precautions, hand hygiene requirements, personal protective equipment (PPE) use, sharps and biohazardous waste management, infection surveillance and reporting, and patient and staff education. Infection prevention is a Condition of Participation under 42 CFR § 484.70, which requires the agency to maintain an infection prevention and control program that is consistent with accepted standards of practice and is designed to prevent the development and transmission of communicable diseases and infections. The home environment presents unique IPC challenges — clinicians provide care in settings they do not control, patients may have infectious conditions requiring transmission-based precautions, and the risk of cross-contamination between patients is a direct function of staff compliance with standard precautions. This policy ensures that Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. maintains a rigorous, evidence-based IPC program compliant with 42 CFR § 484.70, CDC guidelines, OSHA Bloodborne Pathogen Standard, and California Department of Public Health reporting requirements.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all personnel who have direct or indirect contact with patients or patient care materials — including all clinical disciplines (RN, LVN, PT, OT, SLP, MSW, HHA), administrative staff who enter patient homes, and contracted clinical staff.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Standard Precautions shall be followed by all agency staff at every patient encounter. Standard Precautions are the minimum infection prevention practices that apply to all patient care, regardless of suspected or confirmed infection status, and include: (a) hand hygiene; (b) use of personal protective equipment (PPE) based on anticipated exposure; (c) respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette; (d) safe injection practices; (e) safe handling of potentially contaminated equipment or surfaces; (f) sharps safety and disposal.
4.2 Hand hygiene shall be performed: (a) immediately before direct patient contact; (b) before donning gloves for an aseptic procedure; (c) after removal of gloves; (d) after contact with body fluids, non-intact skin, or wound dressings; (e) after contact with the patient's immediate environment; (f) between different care activities on the same patient when moving from a contaminated to a clean body site. Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) with ≥60% alcohol is the preferred method when hands are not visibly soiled. Soap and water shall be used when hands are visibly soiled, after caring for patients with Clostridioides difficile or norovirus, and when ABHR is not available.
4.3 Transmission-Based Precautions shall be implemented in addition to Standard Precautions when caring for patients with known or suspected communicable diseases: (a) Contact Precautions — for MRSA, VRE, C. difficile, scabies, and other contact-transmitted organisms; (b) Droplet Precautions — for influenza, pertussis, and respiratory viruses transmitted by large respiratory droplets; (c) Airborne Precautions — for tuberculosis, measles, varicella, and other airborne-transmitted organisms. The specific precautions for each condition shall follow current CDC guidelines.
4.4 PPE shall be available to all staff and used according to the anticipated exposure: (a) gloves for contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin, mucous membranes, and contaminated surfaces; (b) gowns for procedures likely to generate splashes or when caring for patients on contact precautions; (c) masks and eye protection for procedures that may generate splashes or sprays; (d) N95 respirators for airborne precautions (all staff on airborne precaution assignment must be fit-tested per OSHA requirements).
4.5 All sharps (needles, lancets, scalpels) shall be disposed of immediately after use in a puncture-resistant sharps container. Sharps containers shall be provided to patients receiving injectable medications at home and shall be disposed of per California Health and Safety Code requirements.
4.6 All biohazardous waste generated during home visits shall be managed per OSHA Bloodborne Pathogen Standard (29 CFR § 1910.1030) and RM-PS-002. Clinical waste shall be contained in appropriate biohazard bags, transported safely, and disposed of through the agency's contracted biohazardous waste disposal service.
4.7 The agency shall maintain an infection surveillance program per QA-SM-002 that includes: (a) tracking patient infections (urinary tract infections, wound infections, respiratory infections, CLABSI); (b) trending infection data to identify patterns; (c) reporting notifiable communicable diseases to the California Department of Public Health within required timeframes; (d) reporting infection data to the QAPI program for analysis and performance improvement.
4.8 All staff shall receive initial and annual infection prevention training per HR-TD-001, including: standard precautions, hand hygiene, PPE donning and doffing, sharps safety, bloodborne pathogen exposure procedures, and transmission-based precautions.
4.9 Exposure incidents (needlestick injuries, blood/body fluid exposures) shall be managed per OSHA post-exposure procedures: (a) immediate wound care; (b) reporting to the Director of Nursing within 2 hours; (c) medical evaluation within 2 hours per the agency's occupational health protocol; (d) incident report per RM-ER-002.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Standard Precautions | The minimum infection prevention practices applied during all patient care, based on the principle that all blood, body fluids, secretions, excretions (except sweat), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes may contain transmissible infectious agents. |
| Transmission-Based Precautions | Additional precautions used for patients documented or suspected to be infected with agents that require additional measures beyond Standard Precautions to prevent transmission. |
| Hand Hygiene | A general term referring to handwashing with soap and water, antiseptic hand wash, alcohol-based hand rub, or surgical hand antisepsis. |
| Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) | Equipment worn to minimize exposure to hazards that cause serious workplace injuries and illnesses — including gloves, gowns, masks, face shields, and respirators. |
| Sharps | Any object that can penetrate the skin, including needles, scalpel blades, lancets, broken glass, and broken capillary tubes. |
| Exposure Incident | A specific eye, mouth, other mucous membrane, non-intact skin, or parenteral contact with blood or other potentially infectious material resulting from the performance of an employee's duties. |
| Notifiable Communicable Disease | A disease that is required by law to be reported to the public health department. |
| N95 Respirator | A respiratory protective device designed to achieve a very close facial fit and efficient filtration of airborne particles, required for airborne precautions. |
| Fit Testing | The process of evaluating the adequacy of an N95 respirator's fit on an individual, required by OSHA before initial use and at least annually thereafter. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Standard Precautions at Every Visit

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | All Clinicians | Perform hand hygiene immediately upon entering the patient's home and before any direct patient contact. Use ABHR or soap and water per Section 4.2. | At every visit. |
| 6.1.2 | All Clinicians | Before providing care, assess the anticipated level of exposure and don appropriate PPE: (a) gloves for all procedures involving contact with blood, body fluids, non-intact skin, or wound care; (b) gown if splashing is anticipated or if the patient is on contact precautions; (c) mask and eye protection if splashing or spraying of body fluids is anticipated; (d) N95 respirator if the patient is on airborne precautions. | Before the clinical procedure. |
| 6.1.3 | All Clinicians | Perform hand hygiene immediately after removing PPE, after contact with body fluids, and before touching any personal items or moving to the next patient's home. | After PPE removal and after each patient encounter. |
| 6.1.4 | All Clinicians | Dispose of all used PPE in the appropriate receptacle — regular waste for non-contaminated PPE; biohazard bag for PPE contaminated with blood or body fluids. Do not reuse single-use PPE. | At the conclusion of each procedure. |
| 6.1.5 | All Clinicians | Clean all reusable patient care equipment (stethoscope, blood pressure cuff, pulse oximeter) with an EPA-registered disinfectant between patients. Do not use equipment contaminated from one patient on another patient without cleaning. | Between patients. |

### 6.2 Transmission-Based Precautions

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assigned RN / Director of Nursing | When a patient is known or suspected to have a communicable disease requiring transmission-based precautions, identify the type of precaution required (Contact, Droplet, or Airborne) per CDC guidelines. Document the precaution type in the patient's clinical record and the plan of care. Notify all disciplines and the HHA (if applicable). | At the time of identification or admission. |
| 6.2.2 | All Clinicians | When visiting a patient on Contact Precautions: don gown and gloves before entering the patient's care area; remove and dispose of gown and gloves before leaving; perform hand hygiene; dedicate patient care equipment to the patient or clean between uses. | At every visit with the patient. |
| 6.2.3 | All Clinicians | When visiting a patient on Droplet Precautions: don a surgical mask before entering the patient's care area; maintain the mask throughout the encounter; remove after exiting the care area; perform hand hygiene. | At every visit with the patient. |
| 6.2.4 | All Clinicians | When visiting a patient on Airborne Precautions: don a fit-tested N95 respirator before entering the patient's home; maintain the respirator throughout the visit; remove after exiting the home; perform hand hygiene. Only N95 fit-tested clinicians shall be assigned to airborne precaution patients. | At every visit with the patient. |
| 6.2.5 | Director of Nursing | Schedule patients on transmission-based precautions as the last visit of the day whenever possible to minimize cross-contamination risk. | At scheduling. |

### 6.3 Sharps Safety and Biohazardous Waste

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | All Clinicians | Dispose of all used sharps immediately into a puncture-resistant sharps container. Never recap, bend, break, or hand-pass used needles. | Immediately after use. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN | For patients receiving injectable medications at home (insulin, enoxaparin, etc.), provide a puncture-resistant sharps container and educate the patient/caregiver on: safe disposal of sharps into the container; never placing sharps in household trash; how to obtain a replacement container when full; local disposal options per California guidelines. | At the first visit involving injectable medications. |
| 6.3.3 | All Clinicians | Place all clinical waste contaminated with blood or body fluids in a red biohazard bag. Transport biohazard bags per the agency's transport protocol and dispose through the agency's contracted disposal service per RM-PS-002. | At the conclusion of the visit. |

### 6.4 Exposure Incident Management

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Exposed Employee | If a needlestick or blood/body fluid exposure occurs: (a) immediately clean the exposure site — wash wounds with soap and water; flush eyes with clean water or saline; flush mucous membranes with water; (b) contact the Director of Nursing within 2 hours; (c) report to the agency's designated occupational health provider within 2 hours for medical evaluation and post-exposure prophylaxis assessment. | Immediately; Director of Nursing within 2 hours; medical evaluation within 2 hours. |
| 6.4.2 | Director of Nursing | Ensure the exposed employee receives medical evaluation. Complete an incident report per RM-ER-002. File the OSHA Sharps Injury Log. Document all actions. | Within 24 hours. |

### 6.5 Infection Surveillance and Reporting

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | All Clinicians | When a patient infection is identified during a visit (new wound infection, UTI, respiratory infection, CLABSI), document the findings, notify the physician, and report to the Director of Nursing for infection surveillance tracking. | At the time of identification. |
| 6.5.2 | Director of Nursing | Maintain an infection tracking log documenting: patient identifier, infection type, date identified, treatment, and outcome. Report infection data to the QAPI program quarterly per QA-SM-002. | Ongoing; quarterly reporting. |
| 6.5.3 | Director of Nursing | When a notifiable communicable disease is identified (tuberculosis, hepatitis, COVID-19 per current requirements), report to the California Department of Public Health within the required timeframe (typically within 24 hours for urgent conditions, 7 days for non-urgent). | Per CDPH-required timeframes. |

### 6.6 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Staff member fails to perform hand hygiene | Observing clinician or supervisor addresses immediately | On-site corrective coaching. Director of Nursing notification for repeated violations. Documentation in personnel record. | Immediate coaching; Director of Nursing notification for repeat violations. |
| PPE supplies unavailable for a scheduled visit | Clinician contacts Director of Nursing before the visit | Director of Nursing arranges emergency PPE supply. If PPE cannot be obtained and the visit requires precautions, reschedule the visit. Document the rescheduling reason. | Before the visit; reschedule if PPE unavailable. |
| Needlestick injury occurs | Exposed employee follows Section 6.4 | Immediate wound care; medical evaluation within 2 hours; incident report within 24 hours; OSHA Sharps Injury Log. | Per Section 6.4. |
| Infection cluster identified (2+ patients with the same infection type within 30 days) | Director of Nursing and Compliance Officer | Conduct an investigation for potential cross-contamination. Review clinician hand hygiene compliance, equipment cleaning, and scheduling patterns. Report to QAPI. | Investigation initiated within 48 hours. |

| Appropriate PPE used for all exposure-risk procedures | Direct observation during supervisory visits | ≥95% |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors under Tag G306 (42 CFR § 484.70) will verify: (a) the agency has a written IPC program; (b) staff can describe and demonstrate standard precautions; (c) hand hygiene supplies (ABHR) are carried by staff; (d) transmission-based precautions are in place for qualifying patients; (e) sharps disposal and biohazardous waste management comply with OSHA; (f) infection surveillance data is tracked and reported to QAPI; (g) staff have received IPC training and N95 fit testing as applicable.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hand hygiene not performed between patients | Cross-contamination; infection transmission; survey citation | Provide ABHR to all staff; direct observation during supervisory visits; annual competency |
| Transmission-based precautions not identified or documented | Infection transmission; survey deficiency | Require intake screening for communicable diseases; clinical record alert system |
| Sharps disposal education not provided to patients on injectables | Community safety risk; OSHA violation | EHR checklist for injectable medication patients |
| Exposure incidents not reported | OSHA violation; employee health risk | Annual training on reporting requirements; zero-tolerance for unreported exposures |

## 1. Policy Header

## 2. Purpose
This policy requires individualized patient and caregiver education with documented learning assessments and outcomes at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. Patient education is not ancillary to clinical care — it is a skilled service, a core component of the plan of care, and the primary mechanism through which patients transition from dependency on home health services to independent self-management. A patient who is discharged without the knowledge and skills to manage their condition will return — to the emergency department, to the hospital, or to another episode of home health. Effective education reduces rehospitalization, improves patient outcomes, enhances patient satisfaction, and supports the skilled nature of every visit. This policy ensures that education is planned, individualized, culturally appropriate, delivered using evidence-based adult learning principles, assessed for effectiveness, and documented with the specificity required by CMS surveyors and ADR auditors.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all clinical disciplines — each discipline is responsible for education within their scope: RNs for disease management, medication, safety; PTs for mobility and exercise programs; OTs for ADL techniques and adaptive equipment; SLPs for communication strategies and safe swallowing; MSWs for community resources and psychosocial coping; HHAs for reinforcing education provided by skilled disciplines.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 An individualized Education Plan shall be developed as part of the plan of care for every patient at SOC, identifying: (a) learning needs based on the comprehensive assessment; (b) learning goals; (c) education topics; (d) the patient's and caregiver's preferred learning style (visual, verbal, demonstration, written materials); (e) learning barriers (literacy, language, cognition, vision, hearing, cultural factors); (f) strategies to address identified barriers.
4.2 Patient education shall be provided at every skilled visit, integrated into the clinical care — not delivered as a separate, unrelated activity. Education shall be directly relevant to the visit's clinical purpose and the patient's current status and needs.
4.3 All education shall be documented with specificity sufficient to demonstrate the skilled nature of the teaching. Documentation shall include: (a) the specific topic taught; (b) the teaching method used (verbal instruction, demonstration, teach-back, written materials, video); (c) the patient's/caregiver's response and demonstrated understanding; (d) areas requiring reinforcement; (e) the plan for follow-up education.
4.4 The teach-back method shall be the primary assessment technique: after teaching, the clinician asks the patient/caregiver to demonstrate or explain in their own words what they learned. The teach-back response shall be documented.
4.5 Education materials shall be provided in the patient's primary language per OP-PA-003 and at a literacy level appropriate to the patient's comprehension. Materials shall be culturally appropriate per OP-PA-004.
4.6 Education effectiveness shall be evaluated at each visit by assessing whether the patient can demonstrate or verbalize the taught content. If the patient is not demonstrating learning, the clinician shall modify the education approach (different learning method, shorter sessions, caregiver involvement, simplified content) and document the modification.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Patient Education | The planned, systematic process of providing instruction and counseling to patients and caregivers to promote health, prevent illness, manage chronic conditions, and support self-care after discharge. |
| Self-Management | The patient's ability to independently manage their health condition(s) including medication management, symptom monitoring, dietary management, activity management, and knowing when to seek medical attention. |
| Teach-Back Method | An evidence-based technique for assessing patient understanding by asking the patient to explain or demonstrate what they have been taught, in their own words or actions. |
| Learning Assessment | The evaluation of a patient's current knowledge, skills, readiness to learn, preferred learning style, and barriers to learning. |
| Health Literacy | The degree to which individuals have the ability to find, understand, and use information and services to inform health-related decisions for themselves and others. |
| Education Plan | The documented plan for patient/caregiver education, incorporated into the plan of care, specifying topics, methods, and goals. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Learning Needs Assessment at SOC

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assigned RN | At SOC, conduct a learning needs assessment including: (a) the patient's current knowledge of their diagnosis, medications, and self-management requirements; (b) the patient's preferred learning style; (c) identified barriers to learning (literacy, language, vision, hearing, cognitive status, emotional readiness); (d) the patient's and caregiver's goals for self-management; (e) cultural and spiritual factors affecting learning. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.2 | Assigned RN | Based on the learning needs assessment, develop the Education Plan as part of the plan of care, identifying priority education topics, methods adapted to the patient's learning style and barriers, and target education goals. | Within 24 hours of the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.3 | Assigned RN | Communicate the Education Plan to all disciplines involved in the patient's care per CL-CP-005 so that each discipline can contribute discipline-specific education. | Within 48 hours of SOC. |

### 6.2 Education Delivery at Every Visit

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | All Clinical Disciplines | At every skilled visit, identify at least one education topic relevant to the visit's clinical purpose and the patient's current learning needs. Prioritize education based on patient safety — teach the most critical self-management skills first (when to call 911, medication safety, fall prevention). | At every visit. |
| 6.2.2 | All Clinical Disciplines | Deliver education using the patient's preferred learning method. For complex topics, use multiple methods (verbal explanation + written handout + demonstration). For patients with low health literacy, use plain language, visual aids, and the teach-back method. | During the visit. |
| 6.2.3 | All Clinical Disciplines | After teaching, use the teach-back method: ask the patient to explain or demonstrate what was taught. Document the teach-back response — not just "patient verbalized understanding" but the specific content the patient verbalized or demonstrated (e.g., "Patient correctly stated three signs of wound infection to report: redness spreading beyond the wound edge, purulent drainage, and fever >101°F"). | During the visit. |
| 6.2.4 | All Clinical Disciplines | If the patient is unable to demonstrate understanding after teach-back, modify the education approach: simplify the content, use a different method, break the content into smaller segments, involve the caregiver, or plan for reinforcement at the next visit. Document the barrier identified and the modified approach. | During the visit; follow-up at the next visit. |

### 6.3 Education Documentation

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | All Clinical Disciplines | Document all education in the visit note with the following specificity: (a) Topic: The specific subject taught (e.g., "Insulin injection self-administration technique"); (b) Method: How the education was delivered (e.g., "Verbal instruction with return demonstration"); (c) Content: What was specifically taught (e.g., "Reviewed injection site rotation: abdomen, thighs, upper arms; demonstrated proper angle and technique; reviewed signs of hypoglycemia"); (d) Response: Patient's/caregiver's demonstrated understanding via teach-back (e.g., "Patient correctly demonstrated subcutaneous injection into the abdomen with proper site selection, 90-degree angle, and skin pinch. Patient correctly identified 3 signs of hypoglycemia: shakiness, sweating, confusion."); (e) Plan: Areas for reinforcement at the next visit. | Within 24 hours of the visit. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN | Do not document education in vague terms such as "patient educated on disease process" or "pt verbalized understanding." These notations do not demonstrate skilled education and do not survive surveyor or ADR auditor scrutiny. | At every visit. |

### 6.4 Discharge Education

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Assigned RN | Beginning at least 7 calendar days before anticipated discharge, provide focused discharge education per CL-CP-006, covering: (a) self-management of the patient's primary condition; (b) medication management; (c) diet and activity guidelines; (d) signs and symptoms requiring physician contact or 911; (e) follow-up appointments; (f) community resources; (g) how to access care after discharge. | At least 7 calendar days before discharge. |
| 6.4.2 | Assigned RN | At the final visit, conduct a comprehensive teach-back covering all critical self-management topics. Provide written discharge instructions in the patient's primary language. Document the final education assessment. | At the final visit. |

### 6.5 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Patient unable to learn due to cognitive impairment | Assigned RN notifies Director of Nursing | Redirect education to the caregiver. If no caregiver is available, assess the need for increased visit frequency, HHA services, or community support. Notify physician and MSW. | Within 48 hours. |
| Patient declines education | Assigned RN documents refusal | Document the patient's refusal, the education offered, and the clinical risks of not learning. Continue to offer education at each visit. Notify physician. | At the visit; physician notification within 24 hours. |
| Education documentation is vague or non-specific | Director of Nursing identifies during chart review | Provide documentation coaching with specific examples. Re-audit within 30 days. | Coaching within 7 calendar days. |

## 7. Documentation Requirements

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Learning needs assessment | Documented in the SOC assessment | Assigned RN | EHR — assessment module | At SOC |
| Education Plan | Documented in the plan of care | Assigned RN | EHR — plan of care | Within 24 hours of SOC |
| Education at every visit | Topic, method, content, response, plan documented in visit note per Section 6.3.1 | All clinical disciplines | EHR — visit note | Within 24 hours of each visit |
| Discharge education | Discharge instructions and final teach-back | Assigned RN | EHR — visit note and patient copy | At final visit |
| Written education materials provided | Documentation that materials were provided in the patient's primary language | All clinical disciplines | EHR — visit note | At each education session |
| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment (Appendix A) | Each individual | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Education documented at every skilled visit | Monthly chart audit | ≥95% |
| Education documentation includes topic, method, content, and teach-back response | Chart audit for specificity | ≥90% |
| Learning needs assessment at SOC | SOC chart audit | ≥95% |
| Education materials provided in patient's primary language | Chart audit; patient interview | ≥95% |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors will review visit notes for evidence of patient education — they specifically look for individualized education (not generic), teach-back documentation, and education adapted to the patient's learning needs. Surveyors frequently interview patients to verify that education was provided. ADR auditors will examine whether education documentation supports the skilled nature of the visit — visits where the only skilled component is education must demonstrate that the education required the skills of a licensed clinician.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Patient educated on disease management" — no specifics | Survey deficiency; ADR denial for non-skilled documentation | Structured education documentation template in EHR |
| Same education topics repeated at every visit without adaptation | Suggests education is not individualized or responsive | Require documentation of patient's current knowledge and new topics at each visit |
| Teach-back not performed or documented | Unable to demonstrate education effectiveness | Include teach-back as mandatory visit note field |
| Education not adapted for low health literacy | Ineffective education; patient safety risk | Train all staff on plain language and health literacy-appropriate communication |

# CL-SD-018 — Diabetic Management & Monitoring
## 1. Policy Header

| Field | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Policy ID | CL-SD-018 |
| Policy Title | Diabetic Management & Monitoring |
| Domain | CL — Clinical Operations |
| Subdomain | SD — Service Delivery |
| Classification Tier | ESSENTIAL |
| Status | ACTIVE |
| Review Cycle | Annual |
| Access Tier | Tier 2 — Restricted |
| Policy Owner / Steward | Director of Nursing |
| Effective Date | 2025-07-10 |
| Version | 1.0 |
| Approved By | Governing Body Chair — Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. |
| Last Reviewed | 2025-07-10 |
| Next Review Date | 2026-07-10 |
| Supersedes | N/A (Initial Version) |

## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the assessment, education, monitoring, and documentation standards for the management of patients with diabetes mellitus at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. Diabetes is one of the most prevalent diagnoses in the home health population, affecting approximately 30% of all Medicare home health beneficiaries. Effective diabetic management in the home requires coordinated monitoring of blood glucose, medication management (including insulin administration and oral hypoglycemic agents), dietary education, foot care, complication screening, and self-management training — all of which are skilled services that directly impact patient outcomes, hospitalization rates, and quality measure performance. Poor glycemic management in home health is associated with increased emergency department visits, hospital readmissions, diabetic wound complications, and patient morbidity. This policy ensures that all patients with diabetes receive comprehensive, evidence-based diabetic care integrated into the plan of care.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to all RNs and LVNs providing skilled nursing services to diabetic patients, PTs and OTs whose interventions may affect glycemic control (exercise programs), the Director of Nursing, and Revenue Cycle staff relying on diabetic documentation for coding and billing.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 All patients with a diagnosis of diabetes mellitus shall receive a comprehensive diabetic assessment at SOC, including: (a) diabetes type (Type 1, Type 2, gestational, other); (b) current diabetic medication regimen (insulin, oral agents, injectables) with verification of actual adherence per CL-SD-012; (c) blood glucose monitoring frequency and recent values; (d) HbA1c level (most recent; physician order for new HbA1c if not available within past 3 months); (e) hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia history; (f) diabetic complications screening — retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy, peripheral vascular disease, foot ulcers; (g) dietary assessment — current dietary habits, carbohydrate management, nutritional status; (h) foot assessment — skin integrity, sensation (monofilament testing if available), pulses, deformity, ulceration, callus, toenail condition; (i) patient's and caregiver's current knowledge of diabetes self-management.
4.2 A diabetic management plan shall be developed as part of the plan of care, including: (a) physician-ordered blood glucose monitoring schedule; (b) target blood glucose range per physician parameters; (c) insulin administration schedule (if applicable) with sliding scale or correction factor if ordered; (d) hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia recognition and response protocols; (e) dietary goals; (f) foot care regimen; (g) self-management education goals; (h) exercise recommendations coordinated with PT if applicable.
4.3 At each skilled nursing visit for a diabetic patient, the RN or LVN shall: (a) assess blood glucose per the ordered monitoring schedule; (b) review the patient's blood glucose log since the last visit; (c) assess for symptoms of hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia; (d) assess medication adherence for diabetic medications; (e) perform a focused foot assessment (visual inspection of feet — skin integrity, color, warmth, edema, signs of infection, ulceration); (f) provide targeted diabetic education; (g) document all findings.
4.4 Hypoglycemia (blood glucose <70 mg/dL) and severe hyperglycemia (blood glucose >400 mg/dL or per physician-defined parameters) shall be managed per the physician's orders and the agency's Emergency Glycemic Response Protocol (Appendix A). Physician notification is required within 4 hours for any glycemic emergency managed in the home. If the patient is symptomatic and cannot be stabilized, call 911.
4.5 Insulin administration by agency staff shall follow the medication administration requirements of CL-SD-012, with the additional requirement that blood glucose must be verified immediately before each insulin administration, and the dose must be verified against the physician's insulin order (including sliding scale if applicable) by the administering clinician.
4.6 Patient education for diabetic self-management shall be provided per CL-SD-017 and shall include: (a) blood glucose self-monitoring technique; (b) insulin self-injection technique (if applicable); (c) hypoglycemia and hyperglycemia recognition and response; (d) dietary management including carbohydrate counting or plate method; (e) foot care (daily inspection, proper footwear, when to seek medical attention); (f) sick day management rules; (g) importance of follow-up with endocrinology or primary care.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Hypoglycemia | Blood glucose level <70 mg/dL, which may present with symptoms including shakiness, sweating, confusion, dizziness, irritability, and in severe cases, loss of consciousness or seizure. |
| Hyperglycemia | Blood glucose level above the patient's physician-defined target range, which may present with increased thirst, frequent urination, fatigue, blurred vision, and in severe cases, diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) or hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS). |
| HbA1c (Glycated Hemoglobin) | A laboratory test reflecting the patient's average blood glucose level over the preceding 2–3 months. Target is typically <7% for most adults per ADA guidelines, though individualized targets may be higher for elderly or frail patients. |
| Insulin Sliding Scale | A physician-ordered protocol that specifies insulin doses based on the patient's current blood glucose level, allowing dose adjustment without a new physician order for each dose. |
| Diabetic Foot Assessment | A focused assessment of the feet for skin integrity, sensation, circulation, deformity, infection, and ulceration — a critical component of diabetic care given the high prevalence of diabetic foot complications. |
| Monofilament Testing | A standardized test using a 10-gram monofilament to assess protective sensation in the feet, identifying peripheral neuropathy. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Diabetic Assessment at SOC

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assigned RN | At the SOC visit, complete a comprehensive diabetic assessment per Section 4.1. Document all findings using the Diabetic Assessment Template (Appendix B). | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.2 | Assigned RN | Assess the patient's blood glucose monitoring equipment — verify the meter is calibrated, test strips are not expired, and the patient/caregiver can operate the meter correctly. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.3 | Assigned RN | Conduct a thorough diabetic foot assessment including visual inspection, palpation of pedal pulses (dorsalis pedis, posterior tibial), and sensory assessment. Document all findings. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.4 | Assigned RN | Develop the diabetic management plan per Section 4.2. | Within 24 hours of the SOC visit. |

### 6.2 Ongoing Diabetic Monitoring at Each Visit

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assigned RN / LVN | Assess blood glucose per the physician-ordered monitoring schedule. Document the value, the time of assessment, and the relationship to the patient's last meal (fasting, pre-meal, post-meal). | At each visit per orders. |
| 6.2.2 | Assigned RN / LVN | Review the patient's blood glucose log (home monitoring values since the last visit). Identify patterns: (a) consistent hyperglycemia suggesting medication adjustment needed; (b) hypoglycemic episodes suggesting over-medication or dietary issues; (c) wide glucose variability suggesting monitoring or medication management concerns. Document the review and any patterns identified. | At each visit. |
| 6.2.3 | Assigned RN / LVN | Perform a focused diabetic foot assessment at each nursing visit — at minimum visual inspection. A comprehensive foot assessment (including sensory testing) shall be conducted at each OASIS time point. | Visual at each visit; comprehensive at OASIS time points. |
| 6.2.4 | Assigned RN / LVN | If blood glucose is outside the physician-ordered target range, implement the physician's standing orders (insulin sliding scale if ordered). If blood glucose is <70 mg/dL or >400 mg/dL, follow the Emergency Glycemic Response Protocol (Appendix A). | At the time of glucose assessment. |
| 6.2.5 | Assigned RN / LVN | Provide targeted diabetic education at each visit per CL-SD-017, focusing on the area of greatest need identified during the visit (e.g., if glucose log shows hyperglycemia, focus education on dietary management; if patient has calluses or ill-fitting shoes, focus on foot care). | At each visit. |

### 6.3 Insulin Administration

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN / LVN | Before administering insulin, perform: (a) blood glucose assessment; (b) verification of insulin type, dose, and physician order (including sliding scale calculation if applicable); (c) Seven Rights verification per CL-SD-012; (d) verification of insulin expiration date and storage condition. | Before each insulin administration. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN / LVN | Administer insulin per the physician order using proper technique (correct syringe/pen, correct angle, appropriate injection site rotation). Document: insulin type, dose administered, injection site, blood glucose level before administration, and patient tolerance. | At the time of administration. |
| 6.3.3 | Assigned RN | Teach the patient/caregiver insulin self-injection technique using a systematic approach: demonstration, guided practice, return demonstration, independent practice with supervision. Document competency progression per CL-SD-017. | Beginning at SOC and progressing through the episode. |

### 6.4 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Severe hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) with altered consciousness | Call 911; administer oral glucose or glucagon if available and patient can swallow safely | Emergency medical services; physician notification; incident report per RM-ER-002 | Immediately. |
| Severe hyperglycemia (>400 mg/dL) or symptoms of DKA/HHS | Assigned RN notifies physician immediately; consider 911 | Physician orders; possible emergency transport; incident report | Immediately; physician notification within 1 hour. |
| Blood glucose consistently outside target range for 3+ visits | Assigned RN notifies physician for medication review | Physician adjusts diabetic medication regimen. RN intensifies monitoring and education. | Physician notification within 24 hours. |
| New diabetic foot wound identified | Assigned RN initiates wound assessment per CL-SD-011; notifies physician | Physician orders wound care. Follow CL-SD-011 for wound management. | Physician notification within 24 hours. |

## 7. Documentation Requirements

| Requirement | Document / Record | Responsible Party | Location | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Comprehensive diabetic assessment | Diabetic Assessment Template (Appendix B) | Assigned RN | EHR — assessment module | At SOC and OASIS time points |
| Blood glucose monitoring | Values, time, meal relationship, actions taken | Assigned RN / LVN | EHR — visit note | At each visit per orders |
| Blood glucose log review | Summary of home monitoring values and pattern analysis | Assigned RN / LVN | EHR — visit note | At each visit |
| Diabetic foot assessment | Visual and/or comprehensive foot assessment findings | Assigned RN / LVN | EHR — visit note | At each visit |
| Insulin administration record | Insulin type, dose, site, glucose, patient tolerance | Assigned RN / LVN | EHR — visit note | At each administration |
| Diabetic education | Topic, method, content, teach-back response per CL-SD-017 | Assigned RN / LVN | EHR — visit note | At each visit |
| Glycemic emergency documentation | Glucose value, symptoms, interventions, physician contact, outcome | Assigned RN / LVN | EHR — visit note and incident report | Within 24 hours |
| Policy acknowledgment | Signed acknowledgment (Appendix C) | Each individual | Policy acknowledgment file | Within 14 calendar days |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Comprehensive diabetic assessment at SOC | Chart audit | ≥95% |
| Blood glucose assessed per ordered schedule | Chart audit | ≥95% |
| Foot assessment documented at each nursing visit | Chart audit | ≥95% |
| Diabetic education documented at each visit | Chart audit | ≥95% |
| Glycemic emergencies reported through incident system | Cross-reference visit notes with incident reports | 100% |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors will verify that diabetic management is integrated into the plan of care, that blood glucose monitoring is performed per physician orders, that the agency identifies and manages glycemic emergencies, and that patient education supports self-management. ADR auditors will specifically examine whether diabetic visit documentation supports the skilled nature of the service — glucose checks alone, without clinical analysis and education, may not meet the skilled service threshold.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Blood glucose documented but no clinical analysis of the value or trending | Non-skilled documentation; ADR denial | Train clinicians to analyze each glucose value in context (trending, meal timing, medication adherence) |
| Foot assessment not documented at nursing visits | Missed complications; survey deficiency | Include foot assessment as mandatory field for diabetic patients in visit note template |
| Insulin dose not verified against sliding scale before administration | Medication error risk | Require glucose-to-dose verification documentation for every insulin administration |
| Diabetic education is repetitive and not individualized | Suggests education is not being assessed for effectiveness | Require assessment of current knowledge at each visit before determining education content |
