## 2. Purpose
This policy establishes the standards for respiratory assessment, oxygen therapy management, pulmonary care documentation, and clinical intervention for patients with respiratory conditions at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. Respiratory diagnoses — including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), asthma, pneumonia, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary fibrosis, post-COVID respiratory sequelae, bronchiectasis, lung cancer, and respiratory failure managed at home — represent a significant and clinically complex segment of the Medicare home health population. Respiratory compromise carries the highest risk of rapid clinical deterioration and emergency hospitalization of any chronic condition managed in the home setting. A patient with COPD who is not managing inhaler technique correctly, who does not recognize early exacerbation signs, or whose supplemental oxygen delivery system is malfunctioning may deteriorate from stable to life-threatening within hours. The home environment adds layers of risk — isolated patients, caregiver limitations, equipment failures, and the absence of immediately available emergency clinical resources. This policy ensures that every patient with a respiratory diagnosis receives a comprehensive, evidence-based respiratory assessment at Start of Care, that all oxygen therapy is managed with precision and documented with clinical specificity sufficient to demonstrate skilled nursing care to CMS surveyors and ADR auditors, that respiratory status is monitored at every visit using objective measurement tools, and that deterioration triggers immediate escalation and physician notification. This policy implements the requirements of 42 CFR § 484.60 (plan of care conformance), 42 CFR § 484.75 (skilled professional services), and CMS Home Health Benefit Manual respiratory care coverage requirements.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All registered nurses (RNs) providing skilled nursing to patients with respiratory diagnoses
All licensed vocational nurses (LVNs) providing respiratory monitoring within their California BPC § 2859 scope under RN supervision
All physical therapists (PTs) providing pulmonary rehabilitation and breathing exercise programs
All occupational therapists (OTs) providing energy conservation and ADL adaptation for respiratory patients
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager responsible for respiratory care oversight
Clinical Coordinators managing respiratory patient visit schedules and oxygen vendor coordination
Revenue Cycle staff verifying respiratory documentation supports billed claims
Operations staff coordinating with durable medical equipment (DME) vendors for oxygen and respiratory equipment
This policy governs all skilled nursing and therapy visits for patients with active respiratory diagnoses. It does not separately govern infection prevention standards for respiratory transmissible diseases — those are addressed in CL-SD-016 (Infection Prevention & Control) and RM-EP-001 (Pandemic & Infectious Disease Response), though cross-reference is made where applicable.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 All patients admitted with a primary or secondary respiratory diagnosis shall receive a comprehensive respiratory assessment at SOC, as defined in Section 6.1, incorporating all elements necessary to establish a clinical baseline, develop an individualized respiratory management plan, and accurately complete all applicable OASIS data elements.
4.2 A respiratory management plan shall be developed as part of the physician-approved plan of care for every patient with a respiratory diagnosis, specifying: physician-ordered oxygen therapy parameters (flow rate, delivery device, hours per day); medication regimen (bronchodilators, corticosteroids, antibiotics, mucolytics); breathing exercise program; activity tolerance and energy conservation plan; patient and caregiver education goals; exacerbation recognition and response protocols; and defined parameters for physician notification and emergency response.
4.3 At each skilled nursing visit for a respiratory patient, the RN or LVN shall perform, at minimum: a comprehensive respiratory assessment per Section 6.2; objective measurement of oxygen saturation (SpO2); verification of oxygen therapy compliance and equipment function (if applicable); inhaler technique observation and correction; respiratory medication adherence assessment; and targeted respiratory self-management education.
4.4 Supplemental oxygen shall be administered only per a valid physician order specifying the oxygen flow rate (L/min), delivery device (nasal cannula, simple face mask, Venturi mask, high-flow system), and prescribed hours of use per day (continuous, with exertion only, nocturnal only). The agency shall not modify oxygen flow rates without a physician order, including during exacerbations.
4.5 Oxygen equipment shall be assessed at each visit for: proper function, cleanliness, tubing integrity, patient and caregiver competency in equipment operation, adequate oxygen supply, and safe storage. Any equipment malfunction or supply concern shall be reported to the DME vendor and documented within 24 hours.
4.6 The physician shall be notified within 4 hours (or immediately for emergent findings) when any of the following are identified: SpO2 below the patient's physician-defined threshold (or below 88% if no threshold defined); respiratory rate >24/min at rest; accessory muscle use at rest; new or significantly worsening dyspnea; new or significantly increased productive cough; change in sputum character (color, volume, consistency) suggesting infection; new or worsening fever; signs of respiratory failure (severe dyspnea, cyanosis, altered mental status, inability to complete sentences).
4.7 If the patient presents with signs of acute respiratory emergency (SpO2 <85% despite supplemental oxygen, severe respiratory distress, cyanosis, acute altered mental status), call 911 immediately. Position the patient upright, apply supplemental oxygen at the ordered rate or increase per standing physician order, and notify the physician and Director of Nursing within 2 hours.
4.8 Inhaler technique shall be assessed and corrected at every visit for patients using metered-dose inhalers (MDIs), dry powder inhalers (DPIs), or soft-mist inhalers. Incorrect inhaler technique is one of the leading causes of uncontrolled respiratory disease and preventable exacerbations. The clinician shall document the specific inhaler technique element assessed and corrected at each visit, not simply "inhaler technique reviewed."
4.9 PT involvement shall be initiated per physician order for patients requiring pulmonary rehabilitation exercises, breathing retraining (pursed-lip breathing, diaphragmatic breathing), inspiratory muscle training, functional mobility with respiratory support, and activity tolerance improvement with respiratory monitoring.
4.10 All respiratory patients shall receive a complete respiratory self-management education program per CL-SD-017, covering: exacerbation recognition and action plan; inhaler and nebulizer use technique; oxygen safety and equipment management; energy conservation techniques; pursed-lip breathing and diaphragmatic breathing; avoidance of respiratory triggers; importance of influenza and pneumococcal vaccination; smoking cessation resources (if applicable); and when to call the agency, the physician, or 911.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) | A chronic inflammatory lung disease that causes obstructed airflow from the lungs, encompassing emphysema and chronic bronchitis. |
| Oxygen Saturation (SpO2) | The percentage of hemoglobin binding sites in the bloodstream occupied by oxygen, measured non-invasively by pulse oximetry. Normal range is 95–100%; patients with chronic hypoxemia may have physician-defined lower acceptable thresholds. |
| Supplemental Oxygen Therapy | The administration of oxygen at concentrations above room air (21%) to treat or prevent hypoxemia. Must be physician-ordered with specific flow rate, delivery device, and hours of use. |
| Exacerbation | An acute worsening of respiratory symptoms beyond normal day-to-day variation, sufficient to warrant a change in medication or clinical intervention. Common triggers include respiratory infections, air quality changes, and medication non-adherence. |
| Metered-Dose Inhaler (MDI) | A pressurized canister that delivers a measured dose of medication in aerosol form when activated. Requires specific technique including coordination of actuation and inhalation, optional spacer use. |
| Dry Powder Inhaler (DPI) | An inhaler device that delivers medication in dry powder form. Requires a forceful, deep inhalation technique; not compatible with a spacer. |
| Spacer (Valved Holding Chamber) | A device attached to an MDI that holds the medication aerosol in a chamber, eliminating the need for precise hand-breath coordination and improving drug delivery to the lungs. |
| Nebulizer | A device that converts liquid medication into a fine aerosol mist for inhalation, typically used for patients who cannot effectively use inhalers due to age, cognitive impairment, or severe dyspnea. |
| Pursed-Lip Breathing | A breathing technique in which the patient inhales through the nose for 2 counts and exhales slowly through pursed lips for 4 counts, creating back-pressure that helps keep airways open and reduces air trapping. |
| Diaphragmatic Breathing | A breathing technique that emphasizes use of the diaphragm rather than accessory muscles, reducing the work of breathing and improving respiratory efficiency. |
| Accessory Muscle Use | The recruitment of neck, shoulder, and intercostal muscles to assist with breathing, indicating significant respiratory distress and increased work of breathing. |
| Pursed-Lip Breathing | A controlled breathing technique that reduces the respiratory rate, improves gas exchange, and reduces dyspnea by creating a small amount of back-pressure during exhalation. |
| Pulmonary Rehabilitation | A comprehensive program of exercise training, education, and self-management strategies to improve functional status and quality of life in patients with chronic respiratory disease. |
| Oxygen Concentrator | An electrically powered device that extracts oxygen from room air and delivers it at concentrations of 85–95%, used for patients requiring continuous supplemental oxygen at home. |
| Portable Oxygen System | A compressed oxygen tank or liquid oxygen portable unit used by patients when they leave the home, enabling activity outside the home while maintaining supplemental oxygen. |
| GOLD Classification | The Global Initiative for Chronic Obstructive Lung Disease (GOLD) staging system for COPD severity, based on spirometry results and symptom burden. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Comprehensive Respiratory Assessment at SOC

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Assigned RN | Review all available referral documentation before the SOC visit including: hospital discharge summary (if applicable), pulmonologist or PCP notes, most recent pulmonary function test results, home oxygen prescription, current respiratory medication list, and any recent emergency department visits for respiratory complaints. | Before the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.2 | Assigned RN | At the SOC visit, conduct a comprehensive respiratory assessment documenting all of the following: (a) respiratory diagnosis history — COPD (GOLD classification if known), asthma (severity classification), diagnosis dates, prior hospitalizations and ICU admissions for respiratory causes in the past 12 months; (b) current symptoms at rest and with exertion — dyspnea (rated using the Modified Medical Research Council [mMRC] Dyspnea Scale), cough character and frequency, sputum production (color, volume, consistency), wheezing, chest tightness, hemoptysis; (c) objective measurements — respiratory rate, SpO2 on room air and on supplemental oxygen (if prescribed), blood pressure, heart rate, temperature; (d) respiratory physical examination — auscultation of all lung fields (anterior, posterior, lateral — document location and character of any abnormal sounds including crackles, wheezes, rhonchi, diminished or absent breath sounds); inspection for use of accessory muscles, nasal flaring, pursed-lip breathing, barrel chest, tracheal position, thoracic expansion symmetry; (e) current oxygen therapy — flow rate, delivery device, hours per day, compliance, and equipment type (concentrator, tank, liquid, portable); (f) current inhaler and nebulizer devices — medication names, doses, frequency, patient's demonstrated technique for each device; (g) current oral and systemic respiratory medications (systemic corticosteroids, antibiotics, theophylline, mucolytics); (h) smoking history — current smoker (packs/day), former smoker (pack-year history, quit date), never smoked; (i) respiratory trigger assessment — known triggers (allergens, smoke, dust, cold air, respiratory infections, exertion, strong odors); (j) home environment respiratory assessment — presence of smoke, dust, pets, mold, carpeting, air quality of the home; (k) functional impact of respiratory disease — activity limitation, sleep disturbance, ADL performance, social isolation; (l) prior respiratory treatments — pulmonary rehabilitation participation, prior intubations or mechanical ventilation; (m) vaccination status — influenza (date of last influenza vaccine), pneumococcal (dates of PCV13 and PPSV23 vaccines); (n) current exacerbation status — is this an acute exacerbation or a stable chronic condition? | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.3 | Assigned RN | Assess inhaler technique for each device the patient uses by observing the patient perform the complete inhalation sequence. Use the inhaler-specific technique checklist (Appendix A) for each device type (MDI with and without spacer, DPI, soft-mist inhaler, nebulizer). Document the specific step(s) performed incorrectly and the correction provided. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.4 | Assigned RN | Assess the patient's and caregiver's knowledge of: the respiratory diagnosis and its management; each inhaler and nebulizer device; oxygen therapy safety (if applicable); exacerbation recognition and response; written action plan (if patient has one from their physician). Document the learning needs assessment per CL-SD-017. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.5 | Assigned RN | Assess the home oxygen equipment (if applicable): verify the equipment type and model matches the physician's oxygen prescription; verify that the concentrator is functioning (check the flow rate with a flow meter if available, verify alarm function); assess the tubing for kinks, damage, or contamination; verify the patient's and caregiver's understanding of safe oxygen use (no smoking, keep away from open flames, maintain 5-foot clearance from heat sources); verify adequate oxygen supply (for tank/liquid systems); assess the backup oxygen supply adequacy. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.6 | Assigned RN | Document all SOC respiratory assessment findings using the Respiratory Assessment Template (Appendix B) within 24 hours of the SOC visit, ensuring all elements are captured with sufficient specificity to support accurate OASIS completion and to serve as the clinical baseline for the episode. | Within 24 hours of the SOC visit. |
| 6.1.7 | Assigned RN | Develop the respiratory management plan per Section 4.2 and incorporate it into the plan of care per CL-CP-001. | Within 24 hours of the SOC visit. |

### 6.2 Ongoing Respiratory Assessment and Monitoring at Each Visit

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assigned RN / LVN | At each respiratory patient visit, assess and document all of the following with clinical analysis — not merely data recording: (a) dyspnea rating using the mMRC scale — compare to baseline and prior visit; (b) current respiratory rate — compare to baseline; (c) SpO2 — obtain on room air if the patient is not continuously oxygen-dependent, or on oxygen at the prescribed flow rate; document the measurement conditions (which liter flow, which device, at rest vs. after exertion); (d) lung auscultation — all fields, document location and character of any abnormality; (e) accessory muscle use assessment; (f) cough assessment — productive vs. non-productive, sputum color and volume if productive; (g) patient-reported symptoms since the last visit — dyspnea changes, exacerbation episodes, ER visits, unscheduled physician contacts; (h) oxygen therapy compliance — is the patient wearing oxygen as prescribed? Is the equipment functioning correctly? (i) inhaler and nebulizer use compliance — which devices is the patient actually using, and how frequently? (j) inhaler technique — observe the patient perform technique for at least one device at every visit; document the specific steps assessed and any corrections; (k) medication adherence for all respiratory medications; (l) activity tolerance comparison to prior visit. | At each visit. |
| 6.2.2 | Assigned RN / LVN | Document the respiratory assessment with clinical analysis — compare all findings to baseline and prior visit, analyze clinical trends, identify decompensation indicators, and document the clinical significance of each finding. Example of adequate documentation: "SpO2 84% on 2L NC at rest — below patient's physician threshold of 88%. Increased work of breathing noted — accessory muscle use present. Lung auscultation: diffuse expiratory wheezes bilaterally, diminished at bases. Patient reports increased dyspnea for 2 days, increased yellow sputum production. Physician notified." Example of inadequate documentation: "SpO2 84%, lungs with wheezes, SOB." | Within 24 hours of each visit. |
| 6.2.3 | Assigned RN / LVN | Observe inhaler technique at each visit using the applicable inhaler technique checklist (Appendix A). Identify the specific step requiring correction and provide targeted instruction and supervised practice. Document the specific error corrected, the instruction provided, and the patient's technique after correction. | At each visit. |
| 6.2.4 | Assigned RN / LVN | Verify oxygen equipment function at each visit: check that the concentrator is running and producing flow at the prescribed rate; inspect tubing for kinks, damage, and contamination; verify the patient is using the correct flow setting; verify safe storage and distance from open flames or heat sources; verify adequate tank supply for portable systems. Document findings. | At each visit. |
| 6.2.5 | Assigned RN / LVN | If physician notification criteria per Section 4.6 are triggered, contact the physician within 4 hours and document: the specific trigger finding, the time and method of physician contact, the information communicated, and the physician's response including any new orders. | Within 4 hours of identification. |

### 6.3 Oxygen Therapy Management

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN | Verify that a valid physician order exists for all oxygen therapy before the first visit involving oxygen management. The order must specify: flow rate (L/min), delivery device, and hours of use per day. Contact the physician if any element is missing. | Before the first oxygen-related visit. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN | Assess and document SpO2 on room air AND on supplemental oxygen at the physician-ordered flow rate at each applicable visit. Document both values when clinically feasible. If the patient's SpO2 does not meet the physician's threshold on the prescribed flow rate, contact the physician within 4 hours for orders. | At each visit. |
| 6.3.3 | Assigned RN | Coordinate with the DME vendor for: equipment delivery and setup (if new); equipment malfunction or replacement; filter changes and maintenance; portable oxygen refills; oxygen level monitoring. Document all DME vendor communications and any equipment issues. | As clinically indicated; document within 24 hours. |
| 6.3.4 | Assigned RN | Provide oxygen safety education to the patient and caregiver, documenting the specific safety topics covered: (a) no smoking in the home or within 10 feet of the equipment; (b) keep oxygen equipment at least 5 feet from open flames, gas stoves, candles, and electrical sparks; (c) do not use oil-based lubricants on nasal cannula or mask — use only water-based products; (d) post "Oxygen in Use" signs; (e) do not adjust the flow rate without physician authorization; (f) how to shut off the equipment in an emergency; (g) emergency contact numbers for the DME vendor and the agency. | At SOC; reinforced at each visit where oxygen is managed. |
| 6.3.5 | Assigned RN | Assess the patient's adherence to the prescribed oxygen therapy hours. Document the hours of actual use compared to the prescribed hours. If the patient is using oxygen fewer hours than prescribed, assess the reason (discomfort, equipment issues, knowledge gaps) and implement targeted interventions. | At each visit. |

### 6.4 Respiratory Exacerbation Management

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | Assigned RN / LVN | At each visit, assess whether the patient is experiencing an acute respiratory exacerbation by evaluating: increased dyspnea beyond baseline; change in sputum color from clear/white to yellow, green, or brown; increased sputum volume; increased cough frequency; new fever; decreased activity tolerance compared to recent baseline; SpO2 below the patient's physician-defined threshold. | At each visit. |
| 6.4.2 | Assigned RN / LVN | Classify the exacerbation severity using the GOLD/COPD exacerbation classification or equivalent: (a) Mild — manages with increased use of short-acting bronchodilators only, no change in baseline therapy required; (b) Moderate — requires physician contact for oral corticosteroids and/or antibiotics; (c) Severe — requires emergency department evaluation or hospitalization. | At the time of exacerbation identification. |
| 6.4.3 | Assigned RN | For a moderate exacerbation, contact the physician within 4 hours to report the clinical findings, obtain orders for modified therapy (oral corticosteroids, antibiotics, increased bronchodilator frequency, increased oxygen flow if ordered), and schedule an increased visit frequency if indicated. Document all physician communications and orders. | Within 4 hours of identification. |
| 6.4.4 | Assigned RN | For a severe exacerbation meeting emergency criteria per Section 4.7, call 911 immediately. Position the patient upright (orthopneic position if needed — leaning forward with arms supported). Apply supplemental oxygen at the ordered rate. Do not leave the patient. Notify the physician and Director of Nursing within 2 hours. Complete incident report per RM-ER-002. | Immediately. |
| 6.4.5 | Assigned RN | Following any exacerbation event, conduct a post-exacerbation assessment at the next visit to evaluate the patient's recovery, assess for recurrence risk factors, update the plan of care per CL-CP-002 if needed, and reinforce exacerbation prevention education. | At the next scheduled visit following the exacerbation. |

### 6.5 PT Respiratory Services Integration

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | Physical Therapist | When PT is ordered for a respiratory patient, the PT evaluation shall include: baseline 6-minute walk test (or modified version) with SpO2 monitoring throughout; Borg perceived exertion scale assessment; inspiratory muscle strength assessment; breathing pattern assessment; functional activity assessment with SpO2 monitoring during activities. | At the initial PT evaluation. |
| 6.5.2 | Physical Therapist | Develop a respiratory-specific exercise program that includes: breathing retraining (pursed-lip breathing, diaphragmatic breathing); inspiratory muscle training if indicated; aerobic conditioning at a physician-approved intensity with SpO2 monitoring; functional activity progression; energy conservation strategies. All exercise parameters shall be coordinated with the assigned RN and shall reflect the physician-ordered activity restrictions. | Within 24 hours of the PT evaluation. |
| 6.5.3 | Physical Therapist | At each PT visit, monitor SpO2 before, during, and after exercise. Document the specific SpO2 values at each point. If SpO2 drops below the physician-defined threshold during exercise, reduce the intensity and notify the physician per the escalation protocol. | At each PT visit. |
| 6.5.4 | Physical Therapist | Coordinate exercise recommendations with the assigned RN to ensure consistency between PT exercise guidelines and nursing activity instructions. | Ongoing throughout the episode. |

### 6.6 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SpO2 below physician-defined threshold despite supplemental oxygen at prescribed rate | Assigned RN contacts physician within 4 hours | Physician may order increased flow rate, change in delivery device, laboratory evaluation, or emergency transport. If SpO2 is critically low (<85%), call 911 immediately. Document all actions. | Physician contact within 4 hours; 911 immediately for critical values. |
| Oxygen equipment malfunction (concentrator not producing adequate flow, tubing disconnected, empty tank) | Assigned RN contacts DME vendor immediately; notifies Director of Nursing | DME vendor provides replacement equipment or emergency service. If the patient is in distress, call 911. Document the malfunction, vendor contact, and resolution. | Vendor contact immediately; 911 if patient distress; document within 24 hours. |
| Patient using higher oxygen flow rate than prescribed without physician order | Assigned RN documents and contacts physician | Physician assessment for appropriateness; order obtained if higher flow is medically indicated. If the patient self-adjusted, provide safety education on not adjusting the flow independently. | Physician contact within 24 hours. |
| Patient continues to smoke while on supplemental oxygen therapy | Assigned RN documents and contacts physician and Director of Nursing | Safety education provided regarding fire risk. Director of Nursing assesses whether safe home oxygen therapy can continue. Smoking cessation referral per physician order. If the risk is uncontrollable, Director of Nursing assesses for safety-related discharge per CL-CP-006 Section 6.4. | Patient education immediately; Director of Nursing assessment within 24 hours. |
| Respiratory documentation does not support skilled nursing | Director of Nursing chart review | Documentation coaching with specific examples of analysis-level respiratory documentation. Re-audit within 30 days. | Coaching within 7 calendar days. |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Comprehensive respiratory assessment at SOC with all required elements | Monthly chart audit using Respiratory Assessment Template | ≥95% of respiratory patient SOC records contain complete assessment |
| SpO2 documented at every respiratory patient visit with conditions noted | Chart audit | ≥95% of visits with documented SpO2 and measurement conditions |
| Lung auscultation documented at every respiratory visit | Chart audit | ≥95% of visits with location-specific auscultation findings |
| Inhaler technique assessed and specific findings documented at every visit | Chart audit | ≥95% of visits with device-specific technique documentation |
| Oxygen equipment assessed at every visit for oxygen patients | Chart audit | ≥95% of visits with equipment assessment documentation |
| Physician notified within 4 hours for all trigger criteria events | Communication note audit | ≥95% of trigger events with documented physician notification within 4 hours |
| Respiratory education documented with specificity at each visit | Chart audit for quality of education documentation | ≥90% of visits with topic-specific, teach-back-inclusive education documentation |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors conducting a standard survey under SOM Appendix B will specifically verify under Tag G160 (42 CFR § 484.60) and Tag G184 (42 CFR § 484.75):
1. Evidence that the respiratory assessment is comprehensive and individualized. Surveyors will select respiratory patients and verify that the SOC assessment captures all elements of respiratory function — not merely a SpO2 value and a lung auscultation notation. A comprehensive baseline assessment is the foundation of the skilled nursing justification for the episode.
2. Evidence that oxygen therapy is managed with clinical precision. Surveyors will verify that oxygen prescriptions are on file, that SpO2 is documented at each visit with the liter flow and device noted, and that patients receiving oxygen below their threshold have documented physician notification. Surveyors will specifically look for evidence that the nurse is clinically managing the oxygen therapy rather than merely observing it.
3. Evidence that inhaler technique is taught and assessed — not merely "reviewed." This is the single most common respiratory documentation deficiency. Surveyors consistently cite "inhaler use reviewed" as insufficient — they require documentation of the specific technique elements assessed and corrected. Surveyors may ask patients to demonstrate their inhaler technique during the survey.
4. Evidence that respiratory documentation demonstrates skilled care. ADR auditors from the MAC will deny claims where respiratory visit notes consist only of vital signs and SpO2 values without clinical analysis. The clinician must demonstrate why the visit required the skills of a licensed nurse — analyzing trends, managing complex oxygen therapy, teaching and evaluating inhaler technique, and recognizing early exacerbation signs.
5. Evidence that exacerbations are recognized, managed, and documented. Surveyors will look for evidence that clinical deterioration events triggered physician notification, plan modifications, and appropriate clinical response.
6. Evidence of respiratory self-management education that builds toward independence. Surveyors will compare education documentation across visits — identical education topics at every visit without demonstrated patient progression suggests the education is not individualized or effective.
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| "Inhaler technique reviewed" without specific findings | Survey deficiency; ADR denial for non-skilled documentation | Require inhaler technique checklist completion at each visit; Director of Nursing audits monthly |
| SpO2 documented without noting liter flow and delivery device | Clinical data is uninterpretable; OASIS accuracy risk | EHR visit note template requires liter flow and device fields alongside SpO2 field |
| Oxygen safety education not documented or documented generically | Survey deficiency; patient safety risk | Include oxygen safety as a mandatory education topic at SOC with specific items documented |
| Respiratory assessment consists only of data points without clinical analysis | Non-skilled documentation; ADR denial | Train all clinicians on analysis-level documentation; Director of Nursing monthly chart audit with written feedback |
| Exacerbation identified in visit note but no physician notification documented | Patient safety failure; survey citation | Train clinicians that every exacerbation of moderate or severe severity requires documented physician notification; make physician notification a mandatory field for exacerbation visits |
| Oxygen equipment not assessed at each visit | Equipment failure undetected; patient safety risk | Include equipment assessment checklist as a mandatory field in the visit note template for oxygen patients |
| Patient smoking at home with oxygen — documented but no action taken | Life-threatening fire risk; liability exposure | Require Director of Nursing notification within 24 hours; safety-related discharge assessment if risk persists |

## 10. Training & Acknowledgment Requirements
10.1 All RNs and LVNs providing care to respiratory patients shall receive competency-validated training within 14 calendar days of hire and annually thereafter, covering: comprehensive respiratory assessment technique; SpO2 measurement and clinical interpretation; inhaler technique assessment for all device types (MDI, DPI, soft-mist, nebulizer) with hands-on device demonstration; oxygen therapy management and equipment assessment; exacerbation recognition and classification; emergency respiratory response; respiratory documentation standards demonstrating skilled care; and oxygen safety education.
10.2 All PTs providing pulmonary rehabilitation services shall receive training on SpO2 monitoring during exercise, exercise parameter adjustment based on SpO2 findings, and coordination of respiratory exercise programs with the assigned RN.
10.3 Inhaler technique competency for all respiratory medications used by the agency's patient population shall be validated by the Director of Nursing or designee at hire, using the Inhaler Technique Competency Evaluation Tool (Appendix D), before clinicians independently teach patients inhaler use.
10.4 All personnel within scope of this policy shall sign the Policy Acknowledgment Form (Appendix C) within 14 calendar days of the policy effective date, any revision, or new hire/appointment.
10.5 The Director of Nursing shall maintain training completion and competency records for all clinicians providing respiratory care services and shall report any non-compliance to the Administrator within 7 calendar days of any training deadline.
## 11. Version Control
11.1 This policy is maintained under the agency's enterprise policy lifecycle management system per policy EN-LC-001.
11.2 Only the most current approved version of this policy, as reflected in the policy header, is valid for any operational, compliance, or regulatory purpose. All superseded versions must be archived and clearly marked as "SUPERSEDED — NOT FOR USE."
11.3 Any substantive revision to this policy requires: (a) review and approval by the Governing Body, documented in meeting minutes; (b) re-acknowledgment by all personnel within scope within 14 calendar days of the revised effective date; (c) update to the enterprise policy index per EN-TG-001.
11.4 Non-substantive revisions (formatting, typographical corrections, updated cross-references) may be approved by the Administrator with notification to the Governing Body at the next regular meeting.

## 2. Purpose
This policy defines the age-appropriate assessment standards, service delivery requirements, family and caregiver engagement protocols, and clinical documentation expectations for pediatric patients receiving home health services at Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. Pediatric home health — defined for purposes of this policy as services delivered to patients under the age of 18 — presents clinical, ethical, legal, and regulatory dimensions that are materially distinct from adult home health. Developmental stage drives every clinical decision: the assessment tools, the communication approach, the family engagement strategy, the safety considerations, and the educational methods all differ fundamentally depending on whether the patient is a neonate, an infant, a toddler, a school-age child, or an adolescent. The pediatric patient's legal framework differs as well — informed consent belongs to the parent or legal guardian (with limited exceptions for mature minors and emancipated minors under California law), mandated reporting obligations are heightened, and developmental surveillance is a required component of every assessment. This policy ensures that every pediatric patient receives services that are developmentally appropriate, family-centered, legally compliant, and documented with the clinical specificity required by CMS, the California Department of Public Health, and ADR auditors evaluating whether the service was skilled and medically necessary. This policy implements the requirements of 42 CFR § 484.60 (plan of care conformance), 42 CFR § 484.75 (skilled professional services), and California-specific pediatric home health regulations under Title 22, California Code of Regulations.
## 3. Scope
This policy applies to:
All registered nurses (RNs) and licensed vocational nurses (LVNs) providing skilled nursing to pediatric patients
All physical therapists (PTs) and physical therapist assistants (PTAs) providing pediatric therapy
All occupational therapists (OTs) and certified occupational therapy assistants (COTAs) providing pediatric therapy
All speech-language pathologists (SLPs) providing pediatric services
All medical social workers (MSWs) providing pediatric family support
All home health aides (HHAs) providing pediatric personal care
The Director of Nursing / Clinical Manager
HR staff ensuring pediatric-specific competency validation before pediatric assignment
The Compliance Officer for mandated reporting obligations
This policy applies to all pediatric home health patients aged 0–17 years inclusive. It is a supplemental policy — all applicable adult clinical policies (CL-CP-001 through CL-SD-019) apply to pediatric patients unless this policy specifies a pediatric-specific modification.
## 4. Policy Statement
4.1 Care Indeed Home Health Care, Inc. shall provide pediatric home health services only when the agency has sufficient clinicians with demonstrated pediatric clinical competency to serve the patient safely and effectively. Before accepting a pediatric referral, the Director of Nursing shall verify that: (a) at least one RN with documented pediatric clinical experience is available to manage the case; (b) all disciplines ordered are staffed by clinicians with pediatric experience or supervised by a clinician with pediatric experience; (c) the agency's equipment inventory (pediatric-sized assessment tools, pediatric vital sign reference ranges, pediatric weight-based medication calculations) supports safe pediatric care delivery.
4.2 All pediatric clinical activities — assessments, interventions, education, and documentation — shall be developmentally appropriate for the patient's specific age and developmental stage. The clinician shall document the patient's chronological age and, where clinically relevant (for premature infants and patients with developmental delays), the corrected gestational age.
4.3 Informed consent for all pediatric home health services shall be obtained from the patient's parent or legally appointed guardian, except as provided by California law for emancipated minors (California Family Code § 7002) and mature minors. Consent shall be documented per CL-PR-003 (Informed Consent). For adolescent patients, age-appropriate assent shall be sought and documented, recognizing that assent is not a substitute for parental consent.
4.4 All clinicians providing pediatric services are mandatory reporters under California Penal Code § 11165.7 and shall comply with the agency's mandatory abuse reporting policy (HR-ER-009) and patient rights policy (CL-PR-006) for the identification and reporting of suspected child abuse, neglect, or exploitation. The threshold for reporting suspected child abuse in pediatric home health is lower than in adult settings — any reasonable suspicion, without requiring proof, triggers the mandatory reporting obligation.
4.5 The plan of care for every pediatric patient shall include: (a) developmental surveillance and milestone monitoring appropriate to the patient's age; (b) family and caregiver education and training as primary partners in care; (c) age-appropriate patient education for pediatric patients with the capacity to understand; (d) growth and nutrition monitoring; (e) immunization status documentation; (f) school and developmental program coordination (for school-age children) where applicable.
4.6 Vital sign assessment in pediatric patients shall use age-appropriate reference ranges. Normal vital signs differ significantly across pediatric age groups — reference ranges for neonates, infants, toddlers, school-age children, and adolescents shall be used. No clinician shall assess pediatric vital signs without knowledge of age-appropriate normal ranges for the patient being assessed.
4.7 Weight-based medication dosing is the standard for most pediatric medications. Any medication administered to a pediatric patient by agency staff shall be dose-verified against weight-based dosing calculations, confirmed against the physician order, and double-checked by a second qualified clinician or through the agency's dose verification protocol before administration.
4.8 Family and caregiver engagement is not optional in pediatric home health — it is a clinical necessity. The parent or legal guardian is the primary decision-maker, the primary care provider between visits, and the primary implementer of the care plan. Every visit shall include structured caregiver training, and the plan of care shall reflect the caregiver's competency level and training progress.
## 5. Definitions

| Term | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| Pediatric Patient | For purposes of this policy, any patient under 18 years of age. |
| Neonate | An infant aged 0–28 days. |
| Infant | A child aged 1 month through 12 months. |
| Toddler | A child aged 1–3 years. |
| Preschool-Age Child | A child aged 3–5 years. |
| School-Age Child | A child aged 6–12 years. |
| Adolescent | A patient aged 13–17 years. |
| Corrected Gestational Age | The age of a premature infant calculated from the original due date rather than the birth date; used for developmental milestone assessment in infants born before 37 weeks gestation, typically until 24 months of age. |
| Developmental Surveillance | The ongoing, flexible process of skilled clinical observation of a child's developmental progress at each health encounter, including developmental milestone review, identification of developmental concerns, and referral for developmental evaluation when indicated. |
| Developmental Milestones | The set of functional skills or age-specific tasks that most children can perform within a certain age range, including gross motor, fine motor, language and communication, social-emotional, and cognitive domains. |
| Family-Centered Care | An approach to pediatric health care in which the patient, family, and healthcare providers work in partnership, recognizing the family as the constant in the child's life and as essential partners in clinical decision-making. |
| Informed Assent | The expression of a pediatric patient's willingness to participate in care — typically sought from school-age children and adolescents — acknowledging their developing autonomy, while informed consent remains with the parent or legal guardian. |
| Emancipated Minor | A minor who has been legally freed from parental control by court order, marriage, military service, or financial self-sufficiency, and who may consent to their own medical care under California Family Code § 7002. |
| Weight-Based Dosing | The standard pediatric medication dosing methodology in which the dose is calculated based on the child's current body weight in kilograms, expressed as mg/kg. |
| Mandatory Reporter | Under California Penal Code § 11165.7, a defined category of professional — including all licensed healthcare workers — who is legally required to report known or reasonably suspected child abuse or neglect to law enforcement or a child protective services agency. |

## 6. Procedures
### 6.1 Pediatric Referral Acceptance and Staffing Determination

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.1.1 | Director of Nursing | Upon receipt of a pediatric referral, assess the agency's capacity to accept the case before acceptance: (a) verify that a qualified RN with documented pediatric nursing experience is available to conduct the SOC assessment and manage the case; (b) verify that all ordered disciplines can be staffed by clinicians with pediatric experience; (c) verify that appropriate pediatric assessment tools and equipment are available; (d) assess whether the patient's specific clinical complexity (technology-dependent child, medically fragile neonate, pediatric patient with rare diagnosis) is within the agency's clinical capability. If any capability gap is identified, the Director of Nursing shall determine whether the gap can be filled before accepting or whether the referral must be declined. | Before referral acceptance. |
| 6.1.2 | Director of Nursing | Document the staffing determination, including the names of the assigned clinicians and their pediatric competency status, in the patient's intake record. | At acceptance. |
| 6.1.3 | HR Director / Director of Nursing | Verify that all assigned pediatric clinicians have current pediatric competency validation in their personnel file per HR-WM-007. If a clinician has not been previously assigned to a pediatric patient and lacks documented pediatric competency, arrange for competency validation before the first pediatric visit. | Before first pediatric visit. |

### 6.2 Pediatric SOC Assessment

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.2.1 | Assigned RN | Before the SOC visit, review all available referral information: birth history (for infants and young children), NICU history (if applicable), developmental history, immunization records, prior therapy evaluations, school or early intervention program records (for school-age and preschool children), and the current physician's medical summary. | Before the SOC visit. |
| 6.2.2 | Assigned RN | At the SOC visit, obtain vital signs using age-appropriate technique and reference ranges: (a) Neonates and infants — respiratory rate and heart rate by auscultation or observation for a full 60 seconds; temperature by axillary route (preferred) or temporal artery; blood pressure using age-appropriate cuff; weight measured to the nearest gram (infants) or nearest 0.1 kg (older children); head circumference for children under 2 years; (b) Toddlers through adolescents — blood pressure with age-appropriate cuff size; heart rate and respiratory rate by auscultation; temperature by axillary, tympanic, or oral route appropriate to age; weight to nearest 0.5 kg; height for growth charting. Document all vital signs with age-appropriate normal range notation. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.2.3 | Assigned RN | Conduct a systems-based physical assessment adapted to the patient's age, development, and primary diagnosis, including: (a) Neurological — level of consciousness (age-appropriate alertness, responsiveness, social engagement), tone (hypertonia, hypotonia), symmetry of movement, seizure history and current seizure activity; (b) Respiratory — breath sounds, respiratory pattern, work of breathing, oxygen saturation, tracheostomy or ventilator status (if applicable); (c) Cardiovascular — heart sounds, perfusion, capillary refill, peripheral pulses; (d) Gastrointestinal — feeding method (oral, nasogastric, gastrostomy tube), intake, output, weight trends, constipation or diarrhea; (e) Musculoskeletal — joint range of motion, muscle strength (age-appropriate assessment), contracture risk, positioning equipment needs; (f) Skin — diaper area assessment for infants, skin integrity for immobile patients, stoma sites, central line entry sites, cast or brace sites; (g) Developmental — current developmental milestone achievement compared to age norms; identification of any developmental concerns. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.2.4 | Assigned RN | Conduct a developmental surveillance assessment using a validated screening tool appropriate to the patient's age. For children aged 0–5 years, use the Ages and Stages Questionnaire (ASQ-3) or equivalent. For children aged 5–17 years, use clinical milestone review and the Pediatric Symptom Checklist (PSC) or equivalent. Document the tool used and the results. If developmental concerns are identified, recommend referral to the physician for formal developmental evaluation. | At the SOC visit; findings documented within 24 hours. |
| 6.2.5 | Assigned RN | Conduct a caregiver assessment including: (a) the caregiver's relationship to the patient (parent, guardian, foster parent, other); (b) the caregiver's understanding of the child's diagnosis and care requirements; (c) the caregiver's demonstrated competency in current home care techniques (medication administration, tube feeding, tracheostomy care, wound care — depending on the patient's needs); (d) the caregiver's learning readiness and preferred learning style; (e) the caregiver's physical and emotional capacity to provide care (caregiver stress, fatigue, support system); (f) the home environment's adequacy for the child's safety and care needs. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.2.6 | Assigned RN | Document the immunization status of the pediatric patient, comparing to the current CDC childhood immunization schedule. If immunizations are not current, notify the physician and provide a referral recommendation per the plan of care. | At the SOC visit. |
| 6.2.7 | Assigned RN | Document the SOC assessment using the Pediatric Assessment Template (Appendix A) within 24 hours of the SOC visit. | Within 24 hours. |

### 6.3 Pediatric Plan of Care Development

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.3.1 | Assigned RN | Develop the pediatric plan of care per CL-CP-001, incorporating all pediatric-specific elements per Section 4.5: developmental surveillance plan, family/caregiver training plan, growth and nutrition monitoring plan, immunization status follow-up, and school/developmental program coordination if applicable. | Within 24 hours of the SOC visit. |
| 6.3.2 | Assigned RN | For pediatric patients who are technology-dependent (ventilator, tracheostomy, enteral feeding, PICC line, intrathecal pump), develop a separate Technology-Dependent Patient Care Plan (Appendix B) that specifies: each device, its clinical purpose, the monitoring parameters, the routine maintenance and care schedule, the emergency response plan for device failure, and the caregiver's training requirements for each device. | Within 24 hours of the SOC visit. |
| 6.3.3 | Assigned RN | Goals in the pediatric plan of care shall be expressed in developmentally appropriate, functional, family-centered terms: (a) For infants — goals shall address feeding competency, weight gain, developmental milestone progression, caregiver competency in specific care skills; (b) For toddlers and preschoolers — goals shall address functional mobility, communication, self-care skill development, and caregiver training; (c) For school-age children and adolescents — goals shall incorporate the patient's own goals, school participation, peer interaction, and self-management skill development appropriate to their developmental stage. | At plan of care development. |
| 6.3.4 | Assigned RN | Obtain informed consent from the parent or legal guardian per CL-PR-003 before initiating services. For adolescent patients aged 12 and older, also document the patient's assent. For patients who may be emancipated minors, verify legal status before accepting the minor's own consent. | Before initiating services. |

### 6.4 Pediatric Visit Execution and Caregiver Training

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.4.1 | All Clinical Disciplines | At each pediatric visit, approach the child in a developmentally appropriate manner: (a) Infants and toddlers — speak in a calm, warm tone; include the caregiver in all interactions; explain all procedures to the caregiver before performing them; minimize separation from the caregiver; (b) Preschool and school-age children — explain procedures at an age-appropriate level using simple, concrete language and avoiding threatening words ("hurt," "cut"); allow the child to make simple choices when possible (which arm for blood pressure, which room for the visit); acknowledge the child's feelings; (c) Adolescents — address the patient directly, not only the caregiver; acknowledge their developing autonomy; provide age-appropriate health information directly to the patient; respect their privacy within legal limits. | At each visit. |
| 6.4.2 | All Clinical Disciplines | At each visit, assess developmental milestone progress using observation and caregiver report. Document any milestone delay, regression, or newly identified developmental concern. Notify the physician if a new developmental concern is identified. | At each visit. |
| 6.4.3 | Assigned RN | Provide structured caregiver training at each visit. The caregiver training shall be documented with the same specificity as patient education: what skill was taught, what method was used (demonstration, return demonstration, written materials), the caregiver's demonstrated competency level, and the plan for the next training session. Caregiver training shall progress from observation to guided practice to independent supervised performance to independent competency. | At each visit. |
| 6.4.4 | Assigned RN | Assess the caregiver's stress and coping at each visit. If signs of caregiver burnout, exhaustion, or emotional distress are identified, document the assessment and initiate an MSW referral per CL-SD-005. | At each visit. |

### 6.5 Pediatric Mandatory Reporting

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.5.1 | All Clinical Disciplines | At each visit, observe the child and the home environment for indicators of potential abuse, neglect, or exploitation, including: unexplained injuries or bruising; injuries inconsistent with the explanation provided; multiple injuries in different stages of healing; fearful or avoidant behavior toward caregivers; inadequate supervision; signs of physical neglect (hunger, inadequate clothing, poor hygiene, failure to thrive without a medical explanation); signs of emotional abuse (extreme behavior, withdrawal, low self-esteem); caregiver behavior suggesting abuse potential (hostile, dismissive, excessively controlling, intoxicated). | At every pediatric visit. |
| 6.5.2 | Any Clinician | If reasonable suspicion of child abuse or neglect is identified, the clinician shall: (a) immediately ensure the child's immediate safety at the visit site; (b) report to the Director of Nursing within 2 hours; (c) call the California Child Protective Services (CPS) hotline at 1-800-540-4000 or the local CPS office and make a verbal report within the timeframe required by California Penal Code § 11166 — the report is due immediately upon forming reasonable suspicion, or within 36 hours for non-emergency written report; (d) complete the Suspected Child Abuse Report (SCAR — SS 8572 form) within 36 hours; (e) notify the Compliance Officer per HR-ER-009. The clinician shall NOT investigate the suspected abuse or confront the caregiver — the reporting obligation is triggered by reasonable suspicion alone. | Verbal report immediately upon forming reasonable suspicion; written report within 36 hours. |
| 6.5.3 | Director of Nursing | Upon notification of a suspected child abuse report, immediately ensure the child's safety assessment, coordinate with the Compliance Officer, contact the agency's legal counsel if warranted, and document all actions. Do not interfere with the CPS investigation. | Within 2 hours of notification. |

### 6.6 Pediatric Weight-Based Medication Verification

| Step | Responsible Party | Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 6.6.1 | Assigned RN | For any medication administered to a pediatric patient by agency staff, perform the following verification before administration: (a) obtain the patient's current weight in kilograms (weigh at each visit for infants; weigh monthly for older children or more frequently if clinically indicated); (b) calculate the weight-based dose per the physician's mg/kg order; (c) compare the calculated dose to the physician-ordered dose — if there is a discrepancy exceeding acceptable parameters, contact the physician before administration; (d) perform the Seven Rights verification per CL-SD-012; (e) for high-alert pediatric medications (digoxin, anticoagulants, opioids, chemotherapy, insulin, electrolyte solutions), obtain a double-check verification from the Director of Nursing or designee before administration per RM-PS-005. | Before each pediatric medication administration. |
| 6.6.2 | Assigned RN | Document the weight obtained, the mg/kg calculation, the calculated dose, the ordered dose, the comparison result, and the administration per CL-SD-012. | At each medication administration. |

### 6.7 Escalation and Exception Handling

| Condition | Escalation Path | Corrective Action | Timeframe |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Referral accepted but adequate pediatric competency cannot be confirmed for assigned clinician | Director of Nursing | Assign the case to a more experienced pediatric clinician. Arrange a supervised first visit if the only available clinician has limited pediatric experience. | Before the first visit. |
| Developmental regression identified — child losing previously achieved milestones | Assigned RN notifies physician and Director of Nursing | Physician notified for assessment and referral to developmental pediatrician. Document the specific regression. Plan of care modification per CL-CP-002. | Physician notification within 24 hours. |
| Child appears to have suffered an injury at home — etiology unclear | Assigned RN assesses; considers mandatory reporting | Follow Section 6.5 mandatory reporting protocol. Do not discharge the child to the caregiver's care if imminent danger is suspected — call 911 or CPS. | Immediately. |
| Caregiver unable or unwilling to perform required home care between visits | Director of Nursing and MSW | Assess caregiver competency and barriers. Consider increased visit frequency, additional HHA services, or respite care coordination per physician order. If the child's safety is at risk due to caregiver incapacity, report to CPS and physician. | Assessment within 48 hours. |
| Pediatric weight-based dose calculation results in a dose that differs from the physician's order by more than 10% | Assigned RN contacts physician before administration | Do not administer. Contact physician to clarify the intended dose. Document the discrepancy and the physician's response. | Before administration; physician contact within 2 hours. |

## 8. Compliance & Audit Considerations
### 8.1 How Compliance Is Measured

| Compliance Indicator | Measurement Method | Acceptable Standard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pediatric SOC assessments include all age-appropriate elements | Chart audit using Pediatric Assessment Template | ≥95% of pediatric SOC records complete |
| Developmental surveillance conducted at SOC and OASIS time points | Chart audit | ≥95% of pediatric patients with documented developmental surveillance |
| Caregiver training documented at each visit with specific findings | Chart audit | ≥95% of pediatric visits with specific caregiver training documentation |
| Informed consent obtained before services initiated | Consent form audit | 100% — zero patients without signed parental/guardian consent |
| Weight-based medication verification documented for all pediatric medication administrations | Chart audit | 100% |
| All assigned pediatric clinicians have documented pediatric competency | Personnel file audit | 100% before first pediatric visit |
| Mandatory reporting timeline met for all reported concerns | Compliance file audit | 100% — verbal report within hours; written within 36 hours |

### 8.2 What Surveyors and Auditors Will Look For
CMS surveyors and CDPH surveyors conducting pediatric home health surveys will specifically verify:
1. Clinician pediatric competency. Surveyors will request personnel files for all clinicians assigned to pediatric patients and verify documented pediatric clinical experience and competency validation. Assignment of clinicians without documented pediatric competency is a deficiency.
2. Age-appropriate assessment documentation. Surveyors will examine whether visit notes use adult-oriented templates applied to pediatric patients — this is a frequent deficiency. Assessment findings must be interpreted using age-appropriate normal ranges, and developmental surveillance must be documented.
3. Family-centered care documentation. Surveyors will verify that caregiver training is documented at each visit and that caregiver competency is assessed and tracked. Visit notes that do not document structured caregiver training suggest the service is not being delivered as a skilled home health service.
4. Mandatory reporting compliance. Surveyors may review the agency's training records for mandatory reporting obligations and may inquire about any suspected abuse or neglect situations managed during the survey period.
5. Informed consent from the legal guardian. Surveyors will verify that consent was obtained from the parent or legal guardian, not the minor patient (except for emancipated minors).
### 8.3 Common Failure Points

| Failure Point | Risk | Mitigation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Adult visit note templates applied to pediatric patients without developmental components | Survey deficiency; clinical inadequacy | Develop pediatric-specific EHR visit note template with age-appropriate sections |
| Caregiver training not documented or documented generically | Survey deficiency; family not adequately prepared for home care | Require caregiver training documentation at each pediatric visit as a mandatory field |
| Clinician assigned to pediatric patient without verified pediatric competency | Patient safety risk; survey citation | Director of Nursing reviews all pediatric assignments before the first visit |
| Weight-based medication verification not documented | Patient safety risk; medication error potential | EHR checklist for pediatric medication administration with weight-dose calculation field |
| Mandatory reporting not completed due to uncertainty about whether suspicion is sufficient | Legal violation; child safety risk | Annual mandatory reporting training; threshold is reasonable suspicion — certainty is not required |

## 10. Training & Acknowledgment Requirements
10.1 All clinicians assigned to pediatric patients shall receive competency-validated pediatric-specific training before their first independent pediatric patient visit, covering: age-appropriate vital sign reference ranges and assessment technique; developmental milestone surveillance; family-centered care principles; caregiver training documentation; pediatric weight-based medication dosing and verification; mandatory reporting obligations and reporting thresholds; age-appropriate communication techniques; and pediatric-specific clinical documentation standards.
10.2 Pediatric competency shall be validated through: (a) written knowledge assessment (≥80% passing score) covering pediatric vital sign ranges, developmental milestones, and mandatory reporting requirements; (b) clinical skills demonstration or simulation for pediatric assessment technique.
10.3 Annual refresher training on mandatory reporting obligations shall be provided to all clinical staff per HR-ER-009 regardless of whether they currently serve pediatric patients.
10.4 All personnel within scope shall sign the Policy Acknowledgment Form (Appendix C) within 14 calendar days of the effective date, any revision, or hire.
## 11. Version Control
11.1 This policy is maintained per EN-LC-001. Only the most current approved version is valid. Superseded versions shall be archived as "SUPERSEDED — NOT FOR USE."
11.2 Substantive revisions require Governing Body approval documented in meeting minutes, re-acknowledgment by all personnel within scope within 14 calendar days, and policy index update per EN-TG-001. Note: Given the biennial review cycle for this policy, triggered reviews shall occur any time California mandatory reporting law is amended, CMS pediatric home health guidance is updated, or a pediatric adverse event occurs at the agency.
11.3 Non-substantive revisions may be approved by the Administrator with Governing Body notification at the next regular meeting.
